events.text: The foundation under you is still settling. Seven thousand years is the old measure for this rung, and you feel it in your heels, where the sky has begun to be a floor: not a pain, a patience. Below the clouds a calendar turns over a whole age without noticing you sat still.

choices.text: Sit through another season of it

effects.log: You let the season pass over you like a tide over a stone. Something in the foundation takes one more grain of weight.

choices.text: Walk your edges and test what has set

effects.log: You walk the borders of what you are and press each one. A few hold like iron; one rings hollow, and you mark where.

choices.text: Count the years aloud, to see if it helps

effects.log: It does not help, but it is good company. The counting tires you pleasantly and the foundation takes it for rest.

events.text: A flaw you had forgotten is setting into your foundation along with everything else: a habit of thought from a rung ago, now seven thousand years from being moved. Daeak says it can still be turned if you take it up now, or built into the wall if you do not.

choices.text: Take it up now, and turn it

effects.log: It is slow work and you do it with a patient hand. The habit comes loose in the end, and the foundation closes over a clean seam.

choices.text: Build it in, and make it a feature

effects.log: You choose to live with the flaw and learn its shape. A god who knows their own crack is harder to break than one who pretends to have none.

choices.text: Ask the Silent Hall what it would cost

effects.log: The Hall quotes a price in years and in something else. You write it down and decide to think about it for a long time.

events.text: You wake from a three-year meditation with Daeak's lamp burning at the foot of your seat. They kept it lit the whole time and left a note: the foundation was loud in the night, and they did not want you to wake in the dark.

choices.text: Thank them in person

effects.log: You carry the lamp to their door. They are embarrassed and pleased, and pretend to be neither, and the pantheons are a little warmer after.

choices.text: Keep the lamp lit in turn

effects.log: You keep it burning on your own seat, and the habit settles in. A foundation likes a light in the room.

choices.text: Read the note twice and say nothing

effects.log: You are not good at being cared for yet. You put the note in your sleeve and carry it for the next ten years.

events.text: The gate above you is shut, and the reason is plain: it asks for Mastery of your Dao and a domain of your own, and you do not have it yet. You stand before it every few centuries, as one stands before a locked door in one's own house, and know there is nobody to shout at.

choices.text: Go back to your Dao and work

effects.log: You turn from the gate and walk back toward the root of what you walk. The work is slow, and it is yours.

choices.text: Ask the gate what it saw in you

effects.log: The gate answers in the only language it has, a long silence with a shape. You go home with the shape.

choices.text: Sit at the threshold and wait

effects.log: You wait a decade. Nothing opens, but you notice you have stopped resenting the door.

events.text: Daeak is certain your Dao is deep enough for what is next. The gate disagrees, and the gate has read it more carefully than anyone. It asks for Mastery of your Dao and a domain of your own, and a friend's confidence is not on the list.

choices.text: Thank them and go on trying

effects.log: You thank them for the faith, and keep it separate from the gate. That is harder than it sounds and worth more.

choices.text: Ask them to test you honestly

effects.log: They spar with your Dao for a month, and find three places it is thin. It is the best gift of the century.

choices.text: Be impatient with the gate

effects.log: You push the gate and it does not give. You are not hurt, only a little more tired than before.

events.text: A mortal scholar's prayer asks why a god cannot simply walk through a gate they are strong enough for. You read it twice. The honest answer is that the gate asks for Mastery of your Dao and a domain of your own, not strength, and you are still turning the difference over.

choices.text: Answer in a dream

effects.log: You send the scholar a dream of a door that opens only to the key it was cut for. They wake with the whole matter understood and write it down at once.

choices.text: Keep the prayer by you

effects.log: You put the scholar's question where you can see it, and work with it in your sight. It makes the gate feel less lonely.

choices.text: Pass it to the Heavenly Court

effects.log: The Court files it somewhere deep. A clerk writes back, much later, that nobody has ever answered it so well.

events.text: Daeak tells you, over tea nobody drinks, about the time the gate above this rung turned them back. They went in sure and came out with their sleeves smoking. The lesson was a small one, they say, and took four hundred years to understand.

choices.text: Ask what the lesson was

effects.log: They tell you, and it is smaller than you feared: they had tried to pay with the wrong coin. You write it on the inside of your wrist.

choices.text: Ask what they would do differently

effects.log: They say they would wait. It is not the answer you wanted, and so you suspect it is true.

choices.text: Say you will not fail it

effects.log: They smile with their eyes and say nothing. You will think about that smile for a thousand years.

events.text: You hear that a god one rung above you tried the gate after it and failed. The Silent Hall will not say how. A candle is lit for them in a roadside altar with a single lamp, and the whole pantheon is careful not to look at the candle.

choices.text: Go to the shrine and sit with the candle

effects.log: You sit there an hour. Nobody else comes, and nobody needed to. The candle burns lower and does not go out.

choices.text: Study what is known of the failure

effects.log: You gather what scraps you can of the attempt. It is a map of a cliff, drawn by someone who fell, and you read it carefully.

choices.text: Leave it be

effects.log: You decide a failure belongs to the one who failed. You send a small gift and ask nothing for it.

events.text: You find a record in the Hall of old ascents: a god's account of their own failure at this gate, written for no one. The last page says they stopped trying and simply taught for a thousand years. It reads as if it were the best outcome they could imagine.

choices.text: Copy the last page out by hand

effects.log: You copy the page and pin it above your seat. It reminds you what the climb is for, which is not the climb.

choices.text: Seek out the god who wrote it

effects.log: The god is old and cheerful and has a school of ten thousand. They offer you tea and a seat at the back.

choices.text: Put the record back and go on

effects.log: You put it where you found it. The gate is still in front of you, and you do not mean to teach yet.

events.text: The night before you try the gate, the world is odd. A bell rings in a temple nobody built. Your foundation is the shape of a held breath. You wonder, for the first time in ages, what you would regret not having said to someone.

choices.text: Write it down and leave it on your seat

effects.log: You write two lines on a leaf and leave it on your seat. If it goes well, you will read it and laugh.

choices.text: Say it aloud to the empty hall

effects.log: The hall takes your words and keeps them. It is not the same as saying them to someone, but it is close.

choices.text: Sleep, as mortals do

effects.log: You lie down and let the gate wait. You sleep for the first time in years, deeply, and wake ready.

events.text: On the eve of the gate, Daeak appears at your door with a sealed jar and no explanation. The jar holds an old breeze. "For afterwards," they say, "if you want to remember what it was like to be only this."

choices.text: Take it, and thank them

effects.log: You put the jar on your shelf where you will see it. The breeze inside moves a little when you walk by.

choices.text: Open it now, and let it go

effects.log: The old breeze goes out the window and takes a small knot from your chest. You hadn't known it was there.

choices.text: Refuse; you do not want to look back

effects.log: They accept it without hurt and take the jar away. You wonder, a long while after, whether that was wise.

events.text: A tally of the seven thousand years behind you is the oddest comfort. You list what you learned at each rung, and notice that the best things were not what you were chasing. Tomorrow you try the gate. Tonight you finish the list.

choices.text: Finish the list and read it aloud

effects.log: You read it to the empty hall. It sounds like a life, and it is.

choices.text: Burn the list; you do not need a record

effects.log: The paper takes the flame in one breath. What you learned stays, as it always did, in your hands.

choices.text: Give the list to a young god

effects.log: They take it as a treasure and read it for years. It will be changed by their handwriting, and you are glad.

events.text: Daeak taps a place near your ribs and says there is a hairline in the foundation there. Not a danger, but a place where weather will one day find a way in. It sits in the exact spot where you were proudest.

choices.text: Thank them, and seal it slowly

effects.log: You seal it a drop at a time, and the pride goes out with each drop. It takes a decade.

choices.text: Leave it as a window

effects.log: You decide to keep it as a place where a little light can come in. A flaw that is known stops being a flaw.

choices.text: Pretend you knew already

effects.log: You say you knew. They look at you steadily and say nothing. It is the least honest hour of the century.

events.text: A hollow in your divine foundation shows up only on feast days, when the faithful of a market lane press too close. Your power swells and a little of you thins at the edges, like paper held to a lamp. You do not quite recognize your own voice at the end of the day.

choices.text: Cut the feast days short

effects.log: You shorten the rites and tell the faithful it is for your health. They understand better than you expected.

choices.text: Learn to carry it

effects.log: You learn a way of standing in the crowd that leaves your edges whole. It is a small art and a useful one.

choices.text: Let the thinning teach you what you are for

effects.log: You stay in the crowd and let it thin you, and look at what is left. It is more than you feared and less than you hoped.

events.text: You found a flaw in the way you hold your Dao: it leans toward a valley's weather, and away from the small things that live in it. A divine foundation can tilt for ten thousand years without cracking, and be wrong the whole time.

choices.text: Correct the lean at once

effects.log: You correct the lean and feel the small things come back into view: an ant, a hinge, a loaf of bread. It is startling and good.

choices.text: Study the lean before you correct it

effects.log: You study the tilt for a year. It is a portrait of your own habits, and not one you enjoy.

choices.text: Let a mortal point out what you miss

effects.log: You ask a baker, a ferryman and a child. Each tells you something your Dao should have known.

events.text: You can feel a few valleys of the faithful in the cool quiet of your work: not as sound, but as pressure, like deep water. Today a prayer comes up through it that is more tender than most, and your qi leaps in answer before you have chosen to hear.

choices.text: Answer the prayer gently

effects.log: You send back the smallest sign you can. The qi settles into your foundation like a stone dropped in a calm pond.

choices.text: Let the prayer pass through you

effects.log: You let it go on to whoever it was meant for. Something in you stays lighter for having not kept it.

choices.text: Use the swell for your own work

effects.log: You turn the lift toward your Dao and take a long step. Later you wonder whether it was theirs to give.

events.text: A famine has driven everyone around a market lane to your name, and the prayers are the loudest you have ever heard. Faith like that is a rare strength. It is also the strength of people who have nothing left to spend, and you know what it costs them.

choices.text: Take only what you need, and answer in kind

effects.log: You take a little of the strength and give back rain. The district keeps praying, but now it is thankful rather than desperate.

choices.text: Refuse the strength and send aid

effects.log: You turn the prayers aside and send grain by whatever hands you can find. The qi you forgo is a debt you carry happily.

choices.text: Drink it fully; this is what a god is for

effects.log: You take all of it and the power is staggering. The district prays harder the next year, and you feel the hunger in the words.

events.text: The faithful have taught you by accident. The prayer of a ferry-woman, long and dull and sincere, moves your qi more than a dazzling one. It is the repetition that does it, like a sea against a rock, and you have been waiting for lightning when you should have loved the tide.

choices.text: Sit with the dull prayers and listen

effects.log: You sit with the plain ones all season. By its end the foundation has a smoothness it never had from the great ones.

choices.text: Tell the other gods what you found

effects.log: You tell them at the next gathering. Half of them roll their eyes and half begin that night to listen differently.

choices.text: Keep it as a private craft

effects.log: You say nothing and keep the craft for yourself. It makes you better, and a little more alone.

events.text: Your people have built you a roadside altar with a single lamp. They hang offerings on its rail every dawn, not grand ones: a cut flower, a child's drawing of you with too many arms. The offerings do something for your qi, and something else for your temper.

choices.text: Accept the child's drawing in person

effects.log: You send down a small light. The child forgets everything but the light and tells it for fifty years.

choices.text: Receive the offerings and do nothing

effects.log: You let them hang and the qi take what it takes. The rail grows heavier and the dawns more careful.

choices.text: Ask the priests to stop the drawings

effects.log: They stop. The rail is plainer, and you miss the arms.

events.text: The keeper of a roadside altar with a single lamp has quietly become rich on your name, and the offerings now go through three hands before they reach the altar. You can feel the thinning in your qi. The priest is old, kind to their neighbours and, you think, afraid.

choices.text: Speak to the priest in a dream

effects.log: You say, kindly, that the god knows. The priest wakes and pours the money into the district's well. The offerings thicken.

choices.text: Send an honest priest to work beside them

effects.log: A younger priest arrives and does not preach. Within a decade the books are straight.

choices.text: Ignore it; the qi is still adequate

effects.log: You tell yourself the qi is enough. It is, and the tilt of it makes you quietly ashamed.

events.text: On your festival day, at a roadside altar with a single lamp, a family of strangers leaves no offering at all. They simply sit on the steps and eat, and talk, and let a child nap with her head on a worn stone. Your qi rises more from that than from the heaped altar.

choices.text: Let them stay, and watch over the nap

effects.log: You hold the evening still and warm. The family goes home with a feeling they have no word for.

choices.text: Ask the temple wardens not to disturb them

effects.log: The wardens bow and withdraw. The family never knows that anyone arranged for it.

choices.text: Study what that peace does to the qi

effects.log: You study it a year. It is a gentler engine than awe, and slower, and it does not wear out.

events.text: You have no domain yet, and you feel its absence like a missing tooth. The gods of the twelve each hold one as a hand holds a cup, and you are learning how to want one without needing it. The wanting itself, you suspect, is a part of the trial.

choices.text: Court the domain your Dao answers

effects.log: You go to where the domain is thickest, and sit. It does not notice you, and you cannot tell whether that is rudeness or kindness.

choices.text: Wait; let the domain come to you

effects.log: You work at your Dao and let the question lie. The domain feels you being patient and leans, very slightly, in your direction.

choices.text: Ask a god of a domain how it was for them

effects.log: They tell you, and the answer is weirder than you thought. They say a domain is mostly a promise kept every day.

events.text: At the border of what will one day be a domain, you meet a small god of a tiny, unclaimed thing: the sound a door makes in wind. They have held it for eleven thousand years and are deeply happy. You find yourself envying them, and being surprised at it.

choices.text: Ask them what the door has taught them

effects.log: They talk for three days. The sum is that a small thing, loved, is a whole house.

choices.text: Offer to share a larger share of your own

effects.log: They decline with perfect courtesy. A domain, they say, is not a thing you pour into another cup.

choices.text: Learn the sound of the door

effects.log: You sit in the wind with them and listen. For one afternoon you hear it the way they do.

events.text: You dream of your domain before it exists: a country with weather and a few odd customs, none of which you invented. When you wake, you find you have written some of its laws on the wall in your sleep. They are kinder than the ones you would have chosen awake.

choices.text: Keep them as they are

effects.log: You leave the laws where they are. When the domain comes, it will arrive with a conscience already on the wall.

choices.text: Revise them with a waking head

effects.log: You revise them and make them sharper. In the morning they look like yours, and you miss the others.

choices.text: Copy them and burn the wall

effects.log: You keep the copy and clear the wall. Dreams, you suspect, do not always want to be remembered.

events.text: A Revelation arrives over a market lane the way weather arrives: not as words, but a rearrangement of the air. You spend a month deciphering it and are left with one phrase you cannot stop turning over, like a stone in the mouth. It seems to be about patience.

choices.text: Study the phrase until it opens

effects.log: You study it as one studies a lock. On the thirtieth day it clicks, and the room is bigger.

choices.text: Share it with your pantheon's scribes

effects.log: The scribes receive it with joy and bicker for a year about the grammar. The bickering is itself a kind of study.

choices.text: Keep it, and ask no more of it

effects.log: You decide the phrase is enough. A truth held without being solved has its own warmth.

events.text: A manual of the gods has come into your keeping, copied seven times over by seven tired hands. In the margin of the fourth chapter, someone has written in a different ink: "This does not work near wind through an open door." You are not sure if that is a warning or a joke.

choices.text: Try the chapter anyway

effects.log: You try it. It does not work for you either, and in failing you learn precisely why, which is the useful part.

choices.text: Find out who wrote the note

effects.log: The hand belongs to a god long dead. Their other notes, once found, are better than the book.

choices.text: Write your own note beside it

effects.log: You add a line in the margin: "Try it standing." Somewhere a later god will find it and be glad.

events.text: In the night a Revelation comes that is not for you. It is meant for a young god of the Mountains, and has simply fallen on the wrong roof, here beside a market lane. It is lovely, and it will do you a little good, and it is not yours.

choices.text: Pass it on to the one it was meant for

effects.log: You find the god and hand it over like a dropped glove. They are overwhelmed, and later grateful.

choices.text: Read it and then pass it on

effects.log: You read it first; it teaches you something small about patience. You pass it on a day late and are embarrassed.

choices.text: Keep it

effects.log: You keep it and it does you good. You will never quite forget whose it was.

events.text: A clerk of the Heavenly Court asks you to confirm a line in the Book of Fates: a ferry-woman is to die in their sleep, tonight, at forty. It is a small, ordinary line. You are not required to object. The ink is not quite dry.

choices.text: Confirm it; the Book is the Book

effects.log: You confirm. The line is closed, and you feel the quiet of a rule kept that you would not have written.

choices.text: Ask for a day to consider

effects.log: The clerk gives you the day. You spend it looking at the woman's life, and find nothing to change but the clerk's hurry.

choices.text: Decline to confirm and say why

effects.log: The clerk writes your refusal in the margin and looks frightened. The Book does not change, but a small hesitation enters it.

events.text: You are called as a witness before a Judge of Souls. A ferry-woman you once answered with a small mercy stands accused of selling short measure at a market lane. Your testimony will not decide, but it will weigh. The Judge asks nothing but "What did you see?" and waits.

choices.text: Tell exactly what you saw, and no more

effects.log: You tell it plainly. The Judge writes it down, and the mortal is judged on the truth rather than your fondness.

choices.text: Tell it kindly, and a little more

effects.log: You stretch it by a breath for the mortal. The Judge looks at you and writes nothing; you feel the weight of that silence.

choices.text: Decline to be a witness

effects.log: You say your memory is not a scale. The Judge accepts it, and you walk out lighter and a little ashamed.

events.text: The Court's archivist gives you a rare gift: an hour alone with the Book of Fates, open at your own page. It is blank except for a single line in a small neat hand: "Still to be decided." You find that this is the most comforting sentence you have read.

choices.text: Add nothing, and close the Book

effects.log: You close it gently. A fate unwritten is a door that stays open, and you have no wish to be its carpenter.

choices.text: Write a line, and then rub it out

effects.log: You write a line and see how it would feel. You rub it out. Your hand is cold for a week.

choices.text: Ask the archivist who writes the Book

effects.log: The archivist laughs for a very long time. Then they say, "Whoever remembers longest."

events.text: You spend a century with wind through an open door, the nearest thing to what your Dao answers: you let it slip through your fingers, you taste it, you let it carry you. You discover that the Dao is not the element, but the way the element refuses to be held.

choices.text: Let the element refuse you a while longer

effects.log: You let it slip away again and again. The refusal teaches you something no hold ever could.

choices.text: Give it a gentler grip

effects.log: You stop trying to hold it and learn to cup it. It stays a little longer, then goes, and is warmer for having stayed.

choices.text: Ask your domain's element how it sees you

effects.log: It answers in an image: a small figure standing at the edge of a vast room. You carry the picture for ages.

events.text: You have watched wind through an open door a million times, and today it looks different. It is nothing. It is the same element at a new angle. Your Dao takes a half-step and you are very careful not to move.

choices.text: Hold still until the step finishes

effects.log: You sit through the insight like a deer in a clearing. It finishes with a quiet click, and the world has a new edge.

choices.text: Follow the new angle outward

effects.log: You follow it as far as you can. It ends in a place you cannot name, and you bring back a pebble from it.

choices.text: Write down what you saw

effects.log: You write it as plainly as possible. Later gods will find the page and not understand it, and understand it years later.

events.text: A child at a market lane is playing with wind through an open door, not knowing it. They are doing it badly and joyfully, and a thing you spent a thousand years learning falls out of their hands by accident. You are not sure whether to be annoyed.

choices.text: Watch and learn from the child

effects.log: You watch. The child's way is clumsy and honest, and you steal a trick from it that you will use for centuries.

choices.text: Teach the child gently, from a distance

effects.log: A dream guides their hands a little. They grow up to be a wonderful tinkerer, and never know why.

choices.text: Keep your distance; it is not your lesson

effects.log: You leave the child to the pond. Some playing is better for being unobserved.

events.text: You are asked to give the opening address at a council of pantheons in the Hall of Lamps: a short talk on what a god owes the faithful. The Will of Heaven says order, the Silent Hall says remembrance, the Green Assembly says growth, the Throne of Storms says weight. You must pick, or find a fifth.

choices.text: Speak for order and be heard by the Will

effects.log: You say a god owes a steady hand. The Will of Heaven nods with a light that does not flicker.

choices.text: Speak for remembrance

effects.log: You say a god owes the faithful their dead remembered. The Silent Hall inclines, and no one hears them arrive.

choices.text: Speak for growth and a lighter touch

effects.log: You say a god owes room. The Green Assembly laughs approvingly, and a vine appears in the hall.

events.text: A doctrine you have followed for ages turns out, on a close reading, to be a mistranslation: one word (tend) was swapped by a scribe, and an entire school of devotion built on the swap. The error is beautiful. Correcting it would cost a lot of people their favourite prayer.

choices.text: Publish the correction at once

effects.log: You publish it. There is grief and anger, then a long, honest reformation. The new prayer is plainer and better.

choices.text: Let the error stand and add a footnote

effects.log: You write a footnote that says the old word may be read two ways. It is a compromise, and it holds.

choices.text: Keep it quiet; the prayer is doing good

effects.log: You say nothing. The mistake remains in service of something genuine, and your conscience eats at it for centuries.

events.text: In the Hall of Lamps, a god of the Throne of Storms asks you to explain your doctrine without using any of its words. You try and fail. You try again and succeed halfway. By the end you have learned what you actually believe, which is smaller and truer than the doctrine.

choices.text: Thank them and rewrite your teaching

effects.log: You rewrite it in plain words, and half your students leave. The ones who stay learn faster.

choices.text: Admit that the doctrine is a ladder

effects.log: You say the doctrine is a ladder, and a ladder is not the roof. They smile, and something unclenches.

choices.text: Defend the doctrine out of habit

effects.log: You defend it elegantly. They nod, politely, and leave. You feel as if you had won a point and lost something else.

events.text: You catch yourself at the old etiquette again: the three-step bow and the cup held in two fingers. It is a habit from your Upper Realm centuries, and the gods in the Hall of Lamps are politely baffled. A cup is just a cup here.

choices.text: Drop the habit, with a laugh

effects.log: You laugh at yourself and put the cup down on the grass. A younger god copies you, then decides it is delightful.

choices.text: Keep the habit; it is yours

effects.log: You keep it. It comes to be seen as a charming quirk, and two pantheons adopt a version.

choices.text: Study why it never fits

effects.log: You study the bow and find in it a long-forgotten sorrow. It is a real thing, and it takes a month to put down gently.

events.text: You still keep a ledger of favours owed, a leftover of the immortals' exchange. The oldest line is a pot of tea. A god would never keep one, and when a friend sees it they look briefly hurt. The ledger is accurate to the grain, and entirely beside the point.

choices.text: Burn the ledger and forgive them all

effects.log: The paper goes up warm. You feel suddenly poorer and oddly free, and your friend's smile is returned.

choices.text: Keep the ledger but stop reading it

effects.log: You shelve it. It stays in the drawer like a tooth in a jar, doing nothing, and getting more archaic.

choices.text: Update it with what you now owe

effects.log: You add what you owe in the other direction. The sum is humbling, and it feels honest.

events.text: You flinched at a sunrise today. The Upper Realm taught you to expect a hand behind such things, and the habit lives in the shoulders long after the cause is gone. Here nothing is behind them, and your body has not yet been told.

choices.text: Tell your shoulders, aloud

effects.log: You say it aloud, absurdly. The shoulders drop a hair, and the world goes on being merely the world.

choices.text: Watch it without flinching

effects.log: You sit through it daily for a season. By the end it has become a thing you merely like.

choices.text: Ask a god born here how they learned

effects.log: They say they never had to unlearn anything. You envy them for an hour, then thank them for being what you were trying to become.

events.text: A ferry-woman prays, in a market lane, with a loaf of bread in their other hand. They do not ask for anything. They only say "thank you for the weather." You, who keep weather, find that nobody has ever thanked you for it before.

choices.text: Answer with a small gift of good weather

effects.log: You warm the street by a degree. The mortal looks around, delighted, and eats their bread.

choices.text: Keep the prayer by you

effects.log: You tuck it in a pocket of your attention. It makes the weather-keeping feel like a gift rather than a duty.

choices.text: Ask the mortal what they would change

effects.log: You send a dream. They say, cheerfully, "Nothing, but could it rain on Thursday for the garden?" You put in the rain.

events.text: A prayer reaches you from a ferry-woman who has never believed in gods. "If you are there, I do not need you to do anything. I only wanted to say it out loud, to someone." It is the most honest prayer you have heard in a century.

choices.text: Answer nothing and listen

effects.log: You listen the whole hour. When they have finished you do not move, and they feel it, and sleep easily.

choices.text: Send a quiet sign that he was heard

effects.log: A single leaf lands on their table. They look at it a long time and do not ask why.

choices.text: Ask your pantheon what this is called

effects.log: They have no word. You decide to name it, and the naming teaches you something about listening.

events.text: A mother prays that her child's cough might ease, and the prayer is wrong in an instructive way: she asks the wrong god, for the wrong thing, and misspells your name. It reaches you anyway, because the love in it knows the way. You stay with the wrongness of the address.

choices.text: Answer it yourself

effects.log: You ease it and leave no sign. She will thank the wrong god forever, and you will not correct her.

choices.text: Send the prayer to the god it was meant for

effects.log: You pass it along with a note. The right god answers, grumbling, and sends the mother a remedy.

choices.text: Learn from how love finds the address

effects.log: You study how a misdirected prayer still lands. It is a map of a road you had thought was closed.

events.text: At the noon rite of the Will of Heaven, every god stands in the open and casts no shadow. It is a discipline: nothing hidden, nothing kept back. You find, for the first time, something in yourself that does cast a shadow, and you do not know how to bring it into the light.

choices.text: Bring it out and name it

effects.log: You name it aloud, in the open. The Will inclines, and the shadow, once named, is only a small plain thing.

choices.text: Keep it, and stand carefully

effects.log: You stand so that the shadow falls behind you. It is not a lie, exactly.

choices.text: Ask an elder god what theirs was

effects.log: They tell you, with a little laugh. Everyone has one.

events.text: The Will of Heaven sends a decree: light a dark corner of the world, a valley that has never known a sunrise. It is a noble order and an invasive one. The valley has its own ways of seeing, and no one has asked it.

choices.text: Obey and bring a gentle dawn

effects.log: You bring a pale dawn, slow as a held lamp. The valley adjusts and the order is met.

choices.text: Ask the valley first, in a dream

effects.log: You ask. The valley says it would like a lamp, not a sun. You carry the answer back and the Will bends.

choices.text: Petition the decree

effects.log: You petition. It is read, discussed, and shelved for a thousand years.

events.text: A god of your pantheon hides from the light. They have done something small and unconfessed, and it has made them dim. Everyone can see it and no one speaks. In the Will of Heaven, being seen is the whole law, and they are fading from it.

choices.text: Sit with them and say nothing

effects.log: You sit beside them in the open. Slowly, they brighten, and nobody remarks on it.

choices.text: Tell them to confess

effects.log: You say it kindly and clearly. They confess, and the pantheon is humbler for a season.

choices.text: Leave them to find their own way

effects.log: You leave them. They find it eventually, and avoid you for a century out of embarrassment.

events.text: A doctrine of your pantheon says that a deed unseen is a deed undone. You have done three good things in secret this century, and by the doctrine they do not count. You find, to your surprise, that this makes you furious at the doctrine.

choices.text: Do the next good thing in public

effects.log: You do it where all can see, and it counts. It feels slightly cheap, and the doctrine is satisfied.

choices.text: Argue the doctrine in council

effects.log: You argue. The council is stirred and divides. A fine new line is written.

choices.text: Keep doing them in secret, and let them not count

effects.log: You keep on. They do not count, and you know they happened. That is a kind of cultivation too.

events.text: The Silent Hall keeps a roll of the dead. Today you are asked to read a page of it, and the names are small. A girl of nine, a baker, a lamplighter. You read them aloud. A god of the Hall says "remember" and nothing else, and you do.

choices.text: Read slowly, and remember each

effects.log: You read. By the end you have a handful of lives in your head you did not have at the start.

choices.text: Read well, and sit with the silence after

effects.log: The silence is a kind of honour. You sit in it until the lamp burns low.

choices.text: Add a name nobody had written

effects.log: You add one. The Hall says nothing, and next year the name is on the roll.

events.text: A god of the Silent Hall, who has not spoken in two thousand years, speaks to you. They say a single sentence. It is mundane: a remark about the weather in a country you have never visited. You carry it with you for a century, and it will not stop being profound.

choices.text: Treasure the sentence

effects.log: You treasure it and it becomes a sort of lamp.

choices.text: Answer with a sentence of your own

effects.log: You answer. They nod, and say nothing more, and the Hall counts it a conversation.

choices.text: Ask what they meant

effects.log: They say they only wanted to hear their own voice. You laugh until you cry.

events.text: Silence in the Hall is not emptiness; it is a craft. You are learning to be silent so that others can speak: the pause after a question, the unfilled space beside a griever. You notice you are good at it, and that no one has ever praised you for it.

choices.text: Practise it where it is needed

effects.log: You sit beside griefs for a year. People come away lighter, and never quite know why.

choices.text: Teach it to a young god

effects.log: You teach it. They are terrible at it at first, then, suddenly, not.

choices.text: Keep it as your own quiet art

effects.log: You keep it. It makes you unremarkable and excellent.

events.text: A name has been forgotten: the Hall's roll shows a gap where one used to be. Nobody remembers the person; they only remember that someone was there. The Silent Hall considers this the great sorrow. You are given the task of finding the name.

choices.text: Search the old records for years

effects.log: You find it, in a scrap of a ledger: a ferryman, kind, unremarkable. The Hall welcomes him back.

choices.text: Ask the mortals who might remember

effects.log: Their descendants remember a story, not a name. The story is enough, and the Hall writes it in.

choices.text: Write a new name in the gap, as a placeholder

effects.log: You write a placeholder. It is not honest, and it is kind, and the Hall lets it stand.

events.text: The Green Assembly meets beneath a tree older than the pantheon itself. No one speaks until the tree does, and it speaks in leaves. This year the sentence is one word: "Wait." You are not sure whether it is advice or a description.

choices.text: Wait, and do nothing for a season

effects.log: You wait a season. Things happen anyway; they always do.

choices.text: Ask the tree what to wait for

effects.log: It answers with another leaf. The leaf says "yes."

choices.text: Plant something beside it

effects.log: You plant a sapling at its foot. The tree makes room.

events.text: In the Green Assembly pruning is a sacrament. This year the pantheon asks you to cut back a thing you love: a custom, a corner, a habit of your domain. It is done to help it grow. It is not easy, and you are surprised at how quickly the thing grows back differently.

choices.text: Prune it honestly

effects.log: You prune. A new shape comes, unexpected and sound.

choices.text: Prune it a little, and call it done

effects.log: You prune the lightest cut. It is a partial blessing.

choices.text: Ask another god to do it, so you need not

effects.log: They do it badly, and it is your fault. The thing recovers, not quite as before.

events.text: A young god of the Green Assembly has overgrown: they took on too many domains, too many prayers, and now no one can find their trunk for the leaves. The pantheon watches with that terrible patience it has. You are asked, gently, whether you might help.

choices.text: Help them cut back to the trunk

effects.log: You help. It takes ten years and many tears. The young god flowers in the end.

choices.text: Help them find one thing to love most

effects.log: You ask them what they love. The answer is surprising and small, and they begin there.

choices.text: Leave it to the Assembly's slow way

effects.log: You leave it. The Assembly takes four hundred years. The god survives, grey and wise.

events.text: Compost is the Green Assembly's holiest word. A dead thing becomes a living thing; a lost god becomes a good season. You take your place in the compost procession, and as the others lay down old regrets, you find you have a great heap.

choices.text: Lay them all down

effects.log: You lay them down. The soil takes them. Something in you is lighter than it has been in ages.

choices.text: Lay down a few and keep the rest

effects.log: You keep the ones that still teach you. The procession is gentle with you.

choices.text: Watch the others do it

effects.log: You watch. It is beautiful and you are not ready. They do not ask you to be.

events.text: The Throne of Storms argues in weather: a council is a squall, a verdict a thunderclap. You sit through a long one on the matter of a river's rights. At the end you realise you have understood every word, and that most of them were rain.

choices.text: Speak in your turn, in a gentle drizzle

effects.log: You speak softly, in drizzle. The council quiets and listens, which is its highest honour.

choices.text: Speak in thunder

effects.log: You speak in thunder. You are heard, and slightly feared.

choices.text: Listen the whole way through

effects.log: You listen. The river is given its rights, and you have been a witness.

events.text: A squall of insults arrives from a rival god of your pantheon: wind, hail, a few lightning bolts that miss on purpose. They are not angry exactly; it is the way of the Throne to say a thing with force. You are expected to answer in kind.

choices.text: Answer in kind, with good humour

effects.log: You answer with a gale and a rainbow. The rival laughs, and the pantheon applauds.

choices.text: Answer calmly and let it pass

effects.log: You stay calm. The squall blows out over you and is gone.

choices.text: Withdraw for a season

effects.log: You withdraw. When you return, the rival has forgotten the quarrel and you have not.

events.text: Weight is the Throne's measure of a god: how much remains when the wind is taken out. You are asked to be weighed. A scale of cloud is set up, and you step on it. The needle swings, hesitates, and settles on a number nobody will tell you.

choices.text: Ask for the number

effects.log: They tell you after a long pause. It is neither flattering nor shaming, only true.

choices.text: Refuse to know

effects.log: You step off. The Throne notes it, and honours the refusal as wisdom or cowardice, depending on the god.

choices.text: Weigh someone else

effects.log: You weigh a younger god, and kindly lie by a hair. They are lifted.

events.text: Two of your pantheon's greatest have not spoken in a thousand years, and the weather between them is a permanent storm over a poor country. The Throne asks you to mediate. It is thankless, and the country is under the storm right now.

choices.text: Mediate patiently, season by season

effects.log: You mediate. It takes six decades. The storm breaks into rain and then into spring.

choices.text: Ask the country to forgive them

effects.log: The mortals forgive; the gods are stung into action, and the quarrel ends in embarrassment.

choices.text: Divert the storm to open sea

effects.log: You divert it. The quarrel stays, but the country is spared.

events.text: A child comes to your temple with an unlit lamp and sets it on the step. "It is for when you are ready," they tell the empty air, and run off. You have been a god for a very long time, and nobody has ever told you that you were not ready.

choices.text: Light the lamp at once

effects.log: You light it. It burns with an ordinary flame, and the child never knows it was lit.

choices.text: Leave it unlit and wonder

effects.log: You leave it. The unlit lamp sits on your step and is oddly comforting.

choices.text: Ask the child what you were not ready for

effects.log: You send a dream. The child says, "I do not know. Grown-ups say it." You laugh for a decade.

events.text: Years on, the child comes back, grey at the temples, and stands before the lamp. It is still on your step, and it is still, or again, unlit. They look at it a long moment and ask, quietly, whether you are ready now.

choices.text: Say yes, and let them light it

effects.log: They light it with their own match. The flame is small and wonderfully steady.

choices.text: Say not yet, and ask them to stay

effects.log: They sit down on the step beside the lamp. It is the longest conversation you have had with a mortal.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let the lamp answer

effects.log: The lamp stays dark. They nod, and take it as an answer, and go home calm.

events.text: The child's grandchild finds the lamp on the step of a temple that is now mostly roots and ivy. They light it without asking. It burns like a small wise thing, and the whole forest around it holds still. It is not a god's flame. It is a person's.

choices.text: Take the flame into yourself

effects.log: You take it and feel, for an instant, ready. It does not last, and it is the best instant of the age.

choices.text: Let it burn for them

effects.log: You let it burn through the night. At dawn the roots have made room.

choices.text: Learn from how they lit it

effects.log: They lit it with attention and no ceremony. You note it carefully.

events.text: While copying the Book of Fates you find a misspelling: a mortal's name written with a stroke wrong, so that the fate it governs is slightly off. It is a small error. It will turn a small kindness into a small cruelty in about forty years.

choices.text: Correct the stroke

effects.log: You correct it with a tiny brush. The Book accepts the change without a ripple.

choices.text: Report the error to the Court

effects.log: You report it. The Court thanks you and promises to look into it, which it does, slowly.

choices.text: Leave it and watch

effects.log: You leave it and watch. You are not sure you should have.

events.text: A clerk of the Court finds you in a corridor, red-eyed. It was their stroke, and they have lain awake three nights over it. They are not asking for forgiveness. They are asking whether they should leave the Court, because it seems they cannot be trusted.

choices.text: Tell them every hand slips

effects.log: You say so, plainly. They straighten, and they stay.

choices.text: Offer to check their work for a season

effects.log: You check it. It is spotless, and they learn to trust their own hand.

choices.text: Say they should do as they think best

effects.log: You say it. They think for a long time and leave. You never learn what they chose.

events.text: The clerk, many years on, is a Judge of Souls, and slow, and famed for caution. They send for you. On their desk is a line in the Book, copied perfectly, with a tiny new mark in the margin: a stroke, deliberately wrong, no one would find. "For luck," they say.

choices.text: Smile and say it is the best margin note you know

effects.log: You say so. The Court has a new custom, and none of it was planned.

choices.text: Ask them to leave the page unmarked

effects.log: You ask. They agree, a little sadly, and cleanly strike the mark.

choices.text: Add a mark of your own beside it

effects.log: You add one. The Book now has two small imperfections that mean good will, and a third arrives within the century.

events.text: A mortal student, nine years old, prays a string of questions each night: why the sea is salty, why the sun goes down, why grown-ups sigh. They are not asking you to answer. They are asking the dark. You find you cannot let a question lie unattended.

choices.text: Answer the best question in a dream

effects.log: You answer why the sun goes down. The student wakes and draws it in the dust.

choices.text: Send a teacher into their path

effects.log: A tired schoolmistress finds herself unusually patient that autumn.

choices.text: Listen only, and keep their questions

effects.log: You keep them in a little drawer of attention. They teach you more than you taught them.

events.text: The student is a teacher now, in a one-room school, with a wall chart of "questions we have not answered." Their prayer, tonight, is brief: "Thank you for leaving them open." You feel, with sudden clarity, that it is the best work of your age.

choices.text: Add one question to their wall

effects.log: You send it in a dream. The next morning it is on the wall, in chalk, and they cannot say who wrote it.

choices.text: Leave the wall as it is

effects.log: You leave it. A wall of questions is better than a wall of answers.

choices.text: Bless the school with a quiet year

effects.log: You give it a year of kind weather. Every child that year learns to like learning.

events.text: An envoy of a pantheon hands you a sealed Revelation, and a condition: it is to be opened only after you have lost something that mattered. You hold it in your hands and feel the weight of a thing you have not yet been given a reason to open.

choices.text: Accept it, and put it away

effects.log: You put it in a lacquer box. It sits, patiently, in the corner of your attention.

choices.text: Refuse it for now

effects.log: You refuse. The envoy takes it away, and says it will find you when it is time. You are not sure you will like that.

choices.text: Ask the envoy what is in it

effects.log: They say they do not know. The writer asked only that you be told the rule.

events.text: You have lost something: a long friendship, a domain's corner, a small certainty. It is not a disaster, only a real ache. The sealed Revelation sits in its box, patient. You wonder if this counts. You wonder if anything ever counts.

choices.text: Open the Revelation now

effects.log: You break the seal. The words are in your own handwriting, written ages ago, and they say only: "You are doing better than you think."

choices.text: Wait; this is not yet the loss

effects.log: You wait. It is a loss, and you do not open it, and the waiting is its own kind of faith.

choices.text: Grieve first, and open it after

effects.log: You grieve properly for a season. Afterward the seal opens by itself, as if it had been waiting for you to be finished.

events.text: The sealed Revelation is unsealed now, and its few words have become a quiet part of how you think. A younger god asks if they might see it. It is a private, tender thing, and you are asked to share it. You hold the box in both hands.

choices.text: Share it with them

effects.log: You show them. They read it in silence, and leave with their own sealed box prepared in their mind.

choices.text: Describe it, but keep the words

effects.log: You tell them what it said, not how. They go away with the shape of it, which is enough.

choices.text: Keep it to yourself

effects.log: You close the box. Some words are for one reader, and you are that reader.

events.text: Your first temple was raised without your knowing, by people who had only heard a rumour of you. You find it by accident, on a walk: a small round room, fragrant with incense, with an altar that is slightly too low. Someone has put a cup of water on it.

choices.text: Sit in the room a while

effects.log: You sit. The room is warm, and the faith is plain and gentle, and your qi settles accordingly.

choices.text: Drink the water

effects.log: You drink. It tastes of clay and of someone's careful hands.

choices.text: Fix the altar, quietly, to the right height

effects.log: You raise it a hand's width in the night. The priests call it a miracle and cannot agree on the details.

events.text: You are learning to hear many prayers at once, and it is like listening to a market in a language you almost know. A sound rises from it: someone laughing, in the middle of a prayer, for no reason you can tell. You follow the laugh to a source three provinces away.

choices.text: Join the laugh, silently

effects.log: You laugh with them in the dark. It is the nicest prayer of the year.

choices.text: Ask what they were laughing at

effects.log: They were thanking a god for a bad pun. You are delighted.

choices.text: Note how a laugh carries faith

effects.log: You note it. Laughter is a sturdier carrier than awe.

events.text: A peer offers to share a corner of their domain with you until you win your own, as one lends a spare room. It is a generous offer and it carries obligation. You can feel the weather of the favour already.

choices.text: Accept with open thanks

effects.log: You accept. The corner is warm, and your Dao grows in it like a plant in borrowed soil.

choices.text: Accept, and repay in kind later

effects.log: You accept, and set a mental ledger. It is the first honest one you have kept in ages.

choices.text: Decline; you want to earn your own

effects.log: You decline politely. They nod as if they had expected it. They send a house-warming gift anyway.

events.text: The spirit of a small river, older than your temple, comes to ask you something: whether the new gods are going to move the riverbed. Its voice is a dry reed, and it is truly afraid. You have not had to be reassuring to a river before.

choices.text: Promise to leave the riverbed alone

effects.log: You promise. The river sighs in a pleasing way and begins to sing.

choices.text: Explain the limits of your power honestly

effects.log: You explain what you can and cannot do. The river appreciates it more than a promise.

choices.text: Ask the river how it has survived all the gods

effects.log: It laughs, a trickle. "By being low," it says.

events.text: You teach for the first time. A group of minor spirits asks you to explain your Dao, and you find yourself far less certain than you thought. The questions are good, and you have to keep saying "I do not know, yet." By the end they like you more.

choices.text: Keep teaching as a shared inquiry

effects.log: You make it a seminar. The spirits learn, and so do you.

choices.text: Prepare properly and teach again

effects.log: You prepare and teach better. The second time is a fraction clearer.

choices.text: Stop teaching; you are not ready

effects.log: You stop. The spirits are disappointed, and it is probably wise.

events.text: The foundation under you is still settling. Eight thousand years is the old measure for this rung, and you feel it in the base of your spine, a slow warm weight: not a pain, a patience. Below the clouds a calendar turns over a whole age without noticing you sat still.

choices.text: Let the warmth climb your spine on purpose

effects.log: You breathe into the slow warm weight and let it rise one bone at a time. By the end of the season your back is a banked stove.

choices.text: Take a pan of brine to the salt flat and sit by its boiling

effects.log: You sit with the salt-boiler and watch water give up its salt. Patience, it turns out, is just heat that does not hurry.

events.text: A flaw you had forgotten is setting into your foundation along with everything else: a habit of thought from a rung ago, now eight thousand years from being moved. Hwarin says it can still be turned if you take it up now, or built into the wall if you do not.

choices.text: Burn the old habit out in the Cinder Court

effects.log: You feed it to the court brazier a thought at a time. It smokes, then goes, and leaves the seam clean.

choices.text: Boil it down with the salt-boiler, and keep what is left

effects.log: The flaw crystals out as a hard grey grain. You keep it in a jar as proof you outlasted it.

events.text: You wake from a three-year meditation with Hwarin's lamp burning at the foot of your seat. They kept it lit the whole time and left a note: the foundation was loud in the night, and they did not want you to wake in the dark.

choices.text: Light Hwarin a lamp from your own flame in return

effects.log: You cross the Cinder Court at midnight with a small fire in your hands. Hwarin looks at it a long time and keeps it.

choices.text: Ask the salt-boiler to teach you banking a fire for the night

effects.log: She shows you how coals keep till morning under ash. You bring the knack home like a gift.

events.text: The gate above you is shut, and the reason is plain: it asks for Transcendence in your Dao, and you do not have it yet. You stand before it every few centuries, as one stands before a locked door in one's own house, and know there is nobody to shout at.

choices.text: Take your Dao to the salt flat and test it by burning off what is false

effects.log: You boil your Dao down like brine. What remains is smaller and surer, and the gate seems to notice.

choices.text: Ask Hwarin what Transcendence cost them

effects.log: Hwarin takes the cinder of a burnt letter from their sleeve. You do not ask what it said.

events.text: Hwarin is certain your Dao is deep enough for what is next. The gate disagrees, and the gate has read it more carefully than anyone. It asks for Transcendence in your Dao, and a friend's confidence is not on the list.

choices.text: Take their confidence to the Cinder Court and burn off the extra

effects.log: You let the ash fall until only the part you can use is left. It is warmer than flattery.

choices.text: Ask Hwarin to test your Dao in the court fire

effects.log: They stoke the fire and set your Dao against it. Three places go dark. You note them well.

events.text: A mortal scholar's prayer asks why a god cannot simply walk through a gate they are strong enough for. You read it twice. The honest answer is that the gate asks for Transcendence in your Dao, not strength, and you are still turning the difference over.

choices.text: Answer in a puff of smoke from a salt-lamp

effects.log: The salt-boiler's lamp throws a shape on the wall: a door with a key-shaped hole. The scholar draws it and understands.

choices.text: Ask the scholar to burn the question and bring you the ash

effects.log: They do. The ash spells nothing, and the nothing is a good answer.

events.text: Hwarin tells you, over tea nobody drinks, about the time the gate above this rung turned them back. They went in sure and came out with their sleeves smoking. The lesson was a small one, they say, and took four hundred years to understand.

choices.text: Ask Hwarin to show you the burn mark on their sleeve

effects.log: It is a small scorch, shaped like a door. You trace it with a finger and say nothing.

choices.text: Say you will go in lighter than they did

effects.log: Hwarin laughs and passes the tea. Lighter, they say, is exactly the lesson.

events.text: You hear that a god one rung above you tried the gate after it and failed. The Silent Hall will not say how. A candle is lit for them in a temple with a hundred steps, and the whole pantheon is careful not to look at the candle.

choices.text: Sit with the candle and let your own flame dim a little beside it

effects.log: You turn your fire down in sympathy. The Cinder Court is dim for one evening, and no one says why.

choices.text: Ask Hwarin quietly what the failed god burned

effects.log: Hwarin says: the last of what they were sure of. You learn what to bring up there and what to leave behind.

events.text: You find a record in the Hall of old ascents: a god's account of their own failure at this gate, written for no one. The last page says they stopped trying and simply taught for a thousand years. It reads as if it were the best outcome they could imagine.

choices.text: Copy the last page onto a clay tile and fire it in the Cinder Court

effects.log: The tile comes out hard and red. You set it above your seat where the lamp can reach.

choices.text: Visit the god in their school and learn the first lesson

effects.log: The lesson is how to sit properly in a fire. You are a good student.

events.text: The night before you try the gate, the world is odd. A salt-lamp lights itself. Your foundation is the shape of a held breath. You wonder, for the first time in ages, what you would regret not having said to someone.

choices.text: Light a candle for each person you would have said it to

effects.log: You light eleven and let them burn down. The omen at the salt flat stops, and you sleep.

choices.text: Go to the salt flat at midnight and say it to the lamp that lit itself

effects.log: It flickers once. You have never been so well answered by a thing that cannot speak.

events.text: On the eve of the gate, Hwarin appears at your door with a sealed jar and no explanation. The jar holds an old breeze. "For afterwards," they say, "if you want to remember what it was like to be only this."

choices.text: Take the jar and hang it by the court brazier

effects.log: The breeze inside warms and turns the colour of ember. You keep it lit all year.

choices.text: Open it in the Cinder Court and let the smoke carry it up

effects.log: The breeze lifts the ash into a slow spiral. You stand in it and feel lighter.

events.text: A tally of the eight thousand years behind you is the oddest comfort. You list what you learned at each rung, and notice that the best things were not what you were chasing. Tomorrow you try the gate. Tonight you finish the list.

choices.text: Read the list by the court brazier and strike out what the fire disagrees with

effects.log: Three lines blacken. What survives is shorter and more yours.

choices.text: Feed the list to the salt-lamp one year at a time

effects.log: Each year smokes up a different colour. By the end the lamp is white.

events.text: Hwarin taps a place at the nape of your neck and says there is a hairline in the foundation there. Not a danger, but a place where weather will one day find a way in. It sits in the exact spot where you were proudest.

choices.text: Warm the hairline slowly in the Cinder Court until it fuses

effects.log: Heat takes the crack and melds it. Your pride in the spot cools along with it.

choices.text: Leave the crack as a place for fire to breathe

effects.log: You let a little flame play in it. The flaw turns into a draught that keeps the hearth lit.

events.text: A hollow in your divine foundation shows up only on feast days, when the faithful of a salt flat press too close. Your power swells and a little of you thins at the edges, like paper held to a lamp. You do not quite recognize your own voice at the end of the day.

choices.text: Let the market lane thin you for one hour and no more

effects.log: You stay a single hour among the faithful. You keep your edges and the lane keeps its tune.

choices.text: Bring the feast to the salt flat, where the crowd is spread thin

effects.log: The faithful spread across the white flat in small groups. The pressure comes in waves, not walls.

events.text: You found a flaw in the way you hold your Dao: it leans toward a province of sky, and away from the small things that live in it. A divine foundation can tilt for ten thousand years without cracking, and be wrong the whole time.

choices.text: Light one small lamp in a salt-boiler's shed to test what you notice

effects.log: You notice the grain of the salt, the cracks in the pan, the smell of smoke. The lean eases.

choices.text: Ask the salt-boiler what her days are made of

effects.log: She says: mostly waiting for water. You spend a week waiting for water.

events.text: You can feel a province of prayers in the cool quiet of your work: not as sound, but as pressure, like deep water. Today a prayer comes up through it that is more tender than most, and your qi leaps in answer before you have chosen to hear.

choices.text: Answer with a warm hearth in the prayer's own house

effects.log: Their stove catches at the first match. The qi settles in you like banked coals.

choices.text: Send the prayer on to a god of Fire who needs it more

effects.log: It goes to a young god in a cold temple. They light up, and you feel it in your chest.

events.text: A famine has driven everyone around a salt flat to your name, and the prayers are the loudest you have ever heard. Faith like that is a rare strength. It is also the strength of people who have nothing left to spend, and you know what it costs them.

choices.text: Take a little and answer with a thin fire for cooking and a rain on the salt-pans

effects.log: The pans give salt and the pots boil. The district still prays, but with spoons.

choices.text: Refuse the strength and divert a caravan of grain through the salt flat

effects.log: You turn a caravan with a dream. They arrive at the salt-boiler's door and eat.

choices.text: Take everything, and burn bright

effects.log: You blaze for a season. They pray harder the next year, and you hear the cough in the words.

events.text: The faithful have taught you by accident. The prayer of a salt-boiler, long and dull and sincere, moves your qi more than a dazzling one. It is the repetition that does it, like a sea against a rock, and you have been waiting for lightning when you should have loved the tide.

choices.text: Sit with the ferry-slow prayers by the salt-boiler's fire

effects.log: Her prayer comes every morning at the same pan. You sit till the brine is done.

choices.text: Teach the Cinder Court to keep a plain-prayer hour

effects.log: Hwarin grumbles and then comes. The courts goes quiet for an hour each day.

events.text: Your people have built you a temple with a hundred steps. They hang offerings on its rail every dawn, not grand ones: a pinch of salt, a child's drawing of you with too many arms. The offerings do something for your qi, and something else for your temper.

choices.text: Light the hundred steps one by one for the child who drew you

effects.log: Every step takes a lamp. The child counts them and falls asleep at forty.

choices.text: Send a spark to warm the offering of a pinch of salt

effects.log: It crackles. The priest thinks it is a blessing and tells the whole town.

events.text: The keeper of a temple with a hundred steps has quietly become rich on your name, and the offerings now go through three hands before they reach the altar. You can feel the thinning in your qi. The priest is old, kind to their neighbours and, you think, afraid.

choices.text: Light the keeper's own hearth cold for a night

effects.log: They wake in a cold house and understand. The books are open by dawn.

choices.text: Send the salt-boiler to ask the priest politely for her pinch back

effects.log: She does. The priest weeps, and sends it to her with interest.

events.text: On your festival day, at a temple with a hundred steps, a family of strangers leaves no offering at all. They simply sit on the steps and eat, and talk, and let a child nap with her head on a worn stone. Your qi rises more from that than from the heaped altar.

choices.text: Keep the hundred steps warm for them under the stars

effects.log: Each step glows faintly. The child sleeps like a coal.

choices.text: Have the wardens set out a little salt for their meal

effects.log: The salt-boiler's gift reaches them. They never know whom to thank.

events.text: Your domain stretches now across a province of sky, and a small thing in it happens only because you let it: a late frost holds off, a river changes its mind. You are discovering that a god's power is mostly a list of things they decline to do.

choices.text: Decline one more thing, and write it down

effects.log: You add a line to the list. The domain loosens by a hair, and a field of flowers opens that had not planned to.

choices.text: Reach for a small act of power

effects.log: You do it and the domain bends like cloth. The effect is lovely and slightly alarming.

choices.text: Walk your edges and ask what is owed

effects.log: The edges tell you what they have been carrying. You are ashamed of how long it has been.

events.text: Two of your domain's laws have begun to disagree. The same rain that feeds a field drowns a village below it, and you are the only one who can say which matters more. Hwarin has offered to hold one of the laws for you while you think.

choices.text: Accept, and think a hundred years

effects.log: They hold it. You think. At the end you know the answer is not the one you started with.

choices.text: Decide at once, and bear the consequences

effects.log: You decide and it is done. The village is moved and the field is fed; you attend every wedding of the moved people.

choices.text: Give the law to the village and the field to decide

effects.log: You pass the question down and the mortals find a ditch. It takes them six years. It is better than your answer.

events.text: A god of the silent hall asks to see how you keep your domain. They stay a month, taking notes, asking questions, never praising. On the last day they say your domain is the least beautiful they have seen, and the most alive.

choices.text: Thank them; that is the compliment

effects.log: You thank them and mean it. They go home with a sheaf of notes and a changed way of looking.

choices.text: Ask what they would change

effects.log: They name three things. You change two and keep the one that hurts.

choices.text: Return the visit and take notes in turn

effects.log: You spend a month in their domain being unpraised. It is humbling and enormous fun.

events.text: A Revelation arrives over a salt flat the way weather arrives: not as words, but a rearrangement of the air. You spend a month deciphering it and are left with one phrase you cannot stop turning over, like a stone in the mouth. It seems to be about patience.

choices.text: Let the phrase burn in a salt-lamp until the bright part is clear

effects.log: The flame bends around one word. You keep that word.

choices.text: Carry it to the Cinder Court and read it among the scribes

effects.log: The scribes argue in the heat. A line of the phrase is saved by an ember.

events.text: A manual of the gods has come into your keeping, copied seven times over by seven tired hands. In the margin of the fourth chapter, someone has written in a different ink: "This does not work near a candle flame." You are not sure if that is a warning or a joke.

choices.text: Try the chapter by an open flame and see what the margin meant

effects.log: It works, and does not. The failing half is the wisdom.

choices.text: Trace the note to a scribe of the Cinder Court

effects.log: The scribe is long dead; their other notes are in a salt-cellar. They are excellent.

choices.text: Write beside it: "Works in a draught"

effects.log: A later god will take it as a pun, and then as a method.

events.text: In the night a Revelation comes that is not for you. It is meant for a young god of Fire, and has simply fallen on the wrong roof, here beside a salt flat. It is lovely, and it will do you a little good, and it is not yours.

choices.text: Carry the Revelation across the salt flat to the young god of Fire it was meant for

effects.log: They read it by the brazier and catch alight with joy. You are lightly singed and happy.

choices.text: Read it by the salt-lamp, then burn your notes and deliver it a night late

effects.log: It teaches you something small about patience. You are embarrassed at the delay.

events.text: A clerk of the Heavenly Court asks you to confirm a line in the Book of Fates: a salt-boiler is to die in their sleep, tonight, at forty. It is a small, ordinary line. You are not required to object. The ink is not quite dry.

choices.text: Confirm it, then sit up with the salt-boiler's family beside the pans

effects.log: You sign, and walk down to the flat. You keep the fire lit for them until dawn.

choices.text: Ask the clerk to let her finish the season's boil first

effects.log: The clerk finds a rule that allows a week. She finishes the boil and sleeps well.

events.text: You are called as a witness before a Judge of Souls. A salt-boiler you once answered with a small mercy stands accused of selling short measure at a salt flat. Your testimony will not decide, but it will weigh. The Judge asks nothing but "What did you see?" and waits.

choices.text: Tell exactly what you saw, and let the judge weigh the salt

effects.log: You describe the pan, the scale, the grain. The judgement is just and brief.

choices.text: Ask the court for the salt-boiler's side of the account first

effects.log: You hear it. It changes what you say, in one place.

choices.text: Decline to testify and offer to repay the buyer yourself

effects.log: The judge nods, and the debt is settled between you. The salt-boiler is spared a ruling.

events.text: The Court's archivist gives you a rare gift: an hour alone with the Book of Fates, open at your own page. It is blank except for a single line in a small neat hand: "Ask again later." You find that this is the most comforting sentence you have read.

choices.text: Close the Book and let the line burn in your thoughts

effects.log: It lights slowly, and you sleep with it. A fate unwritten is a fire unlit.

choices.text: Write a line, then burn the page in the Cinder Court

effects.log: It burns to a clean white ash. You rub the ash on your palm.

events.text: You spend a century with a candle flame, the nearest thing to what your Dao answers: you let it slip through your fingers, you taste it, you let it carry you. You discover that the Dao is not the element, but the way the element refuses to be held.

choices.text: Pass your hand through the candle flame until it stops insisting

effects.log: It flees your hand and comes back warmer. You learn what flame is by what it will not be.

choices.text: Carry a flame across the salt flat without letting it gutter

effects.log: It takes a day and your whole attention. The flame is as glad as flames can be.

events.text: You have watched a candle flame a million times, and today it looks different. It is nothing. It is the same element at a new angle. Your Dao takes a half-step and you are very careful not to move.

choices.text: Hold still while the candle bends toward the new angle

effects.log: The flame leans, and you lean with it. The step finishes in warmth.

choices.text: Light a second candle at the new angle and see what the two say

effects.log: Two flames argue and agree. You take a thread of the agreement.

events.text: A child at a salt flat is playing with a candle flame, not knowing it. They are doing it badly and joyfully, and a thing you spent a thousand years learning falls out of their hands by accident. You are not sure whether to be annoyed.

choices.text: Watch the child hold a flame in a salt-pan and learn from the wobble

effects.log: The child's hand shakes and the flame doesn't mind. You steal the shake.

choices.text: Nudge a spark into the child's tinder so it catches the first time

effects.log: It catches. The child cheers and runs to tell someone.

events.text: You are asked to give the opening address at a council of pantheons in the Cinder Court: a short talk on what a god owes the faithful. The Will of Heaven says order, the Silent Hall says remembrance, the Green Assembly says growth, the Throne of Storms says weight. You must pick, or find a fifth.

choices.text: Say a god owes warmth, and light the Cinder Court hearth as you speak

effects.log: The hearth catches. The Throne of Storms approves the fire and the Green Assembly the kindling.

choices.text: Say a god owes the faithful their salt: a little, daily, and never enough to waste

effects.log: The Silent Hall inclines. A salt-boiler in the gallery weeps without knowing why.

events.text: A doctrine you have followed for ages turns out, on a close reading, to be a mistranslation: one word (burn) was swapped by a scribe, and an entire school of devotion built on the swap. The error is beautiful. Correcting it would cost a lot of people their favourite prayer.

choices.text: Publish the correction on the Cinder Court wall in fire

effects.log: The old word burns off the wall. The new one stays. There is a wail and a long recovery.

choices.text: Add a footnote in ash and let the old word stay

effects.log: The footnote smudges. Both words are read, and neither is wrong.

events.text: In the Cinder Court, a god of the Silent Hall asks you to explain your doctrine without using any of its words. You try and fail. You try again and succeed halfway. By the end you have learned what you actually believe, which is smaller and truer than the doctrine.

choices.text: Thank them and rewrite your teaching on a clay tablet, fired in the Cinder Court

effects.log: The plain version bakes hard. Half your students leave; the rest are better.

choices.text: Admit that the doctrine is a flame, not a fire-wall

effects.log: They smile; a hearth in the hall flares in agreement.

events.text: You catch yourself at the old etiquette again: sweeping a doorstep before you sit. It is a habit from your Upper Realm centuries, and the gods in the Cinder Court are politely baffled. A cup is just a cup here.

choices.text: Sweep a different doorstep each morning until the old habit forgets itself

effects.log: You sweep a hundred doorsteps. The habit goes quietly.

choices.text: Keep sweeping, and let the Cinder Court adopt it

effects.log: The court sweeps its own steps. It becomes a custom with a small flame.

events.text: You still keep a ledger of favours owed, a leftover of the immortals' exchange. The oldest line is a borrowed name. A god would never keep one, and when a friend sees it they look briefly hurt. The ledger is accurate to the grain, and entirely beside the point.

choices.text: Hand the ledger to the Cinder Court brazier, page by page

effects.log: Each page lights in a different colour. You are poorer and warmer.

choices.text: Keep it, but write beside each line how it was repaid

effects.log: The ledger becomes a diary. Your friend reads it, moved.

events.text: You flinched at a gold seal today. The Upper Realm taught you to expect a hand behind such things, and the habit lives in the shoulders long after the cause is gone. Here nothing is behind them, and your body has not yet been told.

choices.text: Sit by a candle and let it gutter without flinching

effects.log: It gutters and steadies. Your shoulders drop a hair.

choices.text: Ask Hwarin what flinching felt like in their first age

effects.log: They show a small scar and laugh. You laugh back, and the flinch eases.

events.text: A salt-boiler prays, in a salt flat, with a clay lamp in their other hand. They do not ask for anything. They only say "thank you for the weather." You, who keep weather, find that nobody has ever thanked you for it before.

choices.text: Dry the salt-pans a day early so the salt-boiler gets her rest

effects.log: The salt whitens by noon. She sits on a crate with her bread and is quietly astonished.

choices.text: Ask what she makes of the heat and keep her answer

effects.log: She says it is a good dry sweat. You use the phrase for a century.

events.text: A prayer reaches you from a salt-boiler who has never believed in gods. "If you are there, I do not need you to do anything. I only wanted to say it out loud, to someone." It is the most honest prayer you have heard in a century.

choices.text: Answer nothing and sit with the ferry-woman's lamp until she sleeps

effects.log: You keep it lit at the edge of the dock. She sleeps easily.

choices.text: Send a quiet warmth into her hands

effects.log: Her fingers loosen. She looks at them a long time and does not ask.

events.text: A mother prays that her child's burnt hand might ease, and the prayer is wrong in an instructive way: she asks the wrong god, for the wrong thing, and misspells your name. It reaches you anyway, because the love in it knows the way. You stay with the wrongness of the address.

choices.text: Ease the burnt hand yourself and leave a cool cloth on the sill

effects.log: She thanks the wrong god for a week. You let her.

choices.text: Forward the prayer to the god of Healing with a note about salt

effects.log: He is gruff and quick. The mother gets a salve.

choices.text: Follow the prayer to the mother and see how she words it

effects.log: Her words are crooked and perfect. You steal the shape.

events.text: You hold the domain of War, and you have learned that its sharpest part is the moment before: a banner lifted, a drum not yet struck. Standing in that held breath, you could end a war with a gesture you have not made, and you wonder what the gesture would cost.

choices.text: Make the gesture and end it

effects.log: You make it. Ten thousand soldiers lower their spears at once and are ashamed and relieved in the same breath.
