choices.text: Keep the held breath as a useful fear

effects.log: You keep it. Wars in your domain begin late and end sooner, and nobody thanks you.

choices.text: Study the held breath for its own worth

effects.log: You sit in it for a century. It is the stillest place in the domain.

events.text: Two armies pray to you at once, each for victory, and your temples stand in both camps. Their priests ask for a sign. You have the whole banner-field of War to answer with, and only one honest thing to say.

choices.text: Send both the same sign: go home

effects.log: A single grey dawn falls on both camps. Half of each army takes it as a rebuke and the other half as a gift.

choices.text: Favour the army with the more just cause

effects.log: You judge and tip it, quietly. The result is clean, and you hold it against yourself.

choices.text: Stay silent and let the field decide

effects.log: You say nothing and the field decides. Both temples hold a long, hard quiet afterward.

events.text: Your domain of the Sky teaches you through a single cloud, which holds its shape by never holding it. You watch one for a year and fail to catch the instant it changes. It turns out the changing is the cloud.

choices.text: Let the cloud teach you to loosen

effects.log: You loosen your hold on three old certainties. The Sky feels a little wider around you.

choices.text: Ask Cheonho how the stars are hung

effects.log: Cheonho laughs and says "with the hand open." It is both a joke and a method.

choices.text: Make a cloud of your own

effects.log: It comes out a lopsided shape, and children name it for a rabbit. You are quietly proud.

events.text: Stars are going out over a coast you keep. Only a mortal astronomer has noticed, and she has written to every temple she knows with no reply. It is not a disaster. It is a small error in your accounts, and she is right.

choices.text: Answer her letter in your own hand

effects.log: You write to her in light, across the night. She weeps and then recalculates.

choices.text: Quietly relight the stars

effects.log: You relight them one by one. She will never be sure she was right, and will be right anyway.

choices.text: Ask why they went out

effects.log: You learn it is your own inattention. The correction is humbling, and the Sky is clearer after.

events.text: Every hearth in the world answers a little when you pass, for you hold Fire. You pass a poor kitchen where a mother is coaxing a flame from damp wood, and the flame leans toward you. It is not asking. It is only glad.

choices.text: Help the flame, gently

effects.log: The wood dries and catches. The mother gives thanks to the weather.

choices.text: Let the flame lean and learn from it

effects.log: You study how a small fire leans. It is the oldest lesson in the domain.

choices.text: Pass by; some fires must be earned

effects.log: You walk on. The mother lights it herself within the hour, and it burns better for the effort.

events.text: A hearth-keeper prays for a fire that does not hurt: a flame a child could hold. It is an odd request, and strictly impossible, and it will not leave you alone. You hold Fire; surely you can bend the rules of your own element.

choices.text: Make a flame that warms and never burns

effects.log: You make it, with great effort, and it holds one night. The child holds it and laughs, and the flame goes out like a sigh.

choices.text: Teach the keeper to shield small hands

effects.log: You send a dream of a clay cup around the flame. The keeper wakes and makes one.

choices.text: Refuse; a fire that cannot hurt is not a fire

effects.log: You decline. It sits in you as a hard small principle.

events.text: Death is yours, and you find it is not an end but a door that is always open at a certain hour. You stand in that doorway while a mortal passes through, and see that they are not afraid. It surprises you how much that matters.

choices.text: Hold the door gently

effects.log: You hold it. The mortal goes through with a nod, and the hour is lighter.

choices.text: Ask the passing soul what they saw

effects.log: They tell you, in two words. You keep the words for centuries.

choices.text: Close the door early for another

effects.log: You close it a minute early and open it again. A small mercy that no rule had written.

events.text: A very old mortal prays that you will not come yet: she has one thing unfinished, a quilt, for a granddaughter's wedding. It is a small, fair thing to ask, and no one in the Silent Hall has ever done it twice.

choices.text: Let her finish the quilt

effects.log: You wait on her doorstep a season. The quilt is the best made in the province, and she goes calmly.

choices.text: Send an apprentice to help

effects.log: You send a young dreamer to sew beside her. The quilt is done, and the apprentice learns something.

choices.text: Come at the hour, as you must

effects.log: You come on time. The quilt is unfinished and the granddaughter finishes it. You feel the weight of your own punctuality.

events.text: Every thread in the world runs a little through your fingers, for you hold Fate. Tonight you notice that two threads, long parallel, have begun to lean toward each other. No one has arranged it. They simply lean, as plants lean.

choices.text: Let them meet

effects.log: You let them. Somewhere two strangers share an umbrella, and think nothing of it for years.

choices.text: Study how threads choose

effects.log: You study it a decade. Threads, it turns out, have preferences, and fate is mostly a list of them.

choices.text: Nudge them gently apart

effects.log: You nudge. They lean back toward each other within the year. You give up, a little amused.

events.text: A weaver prays for a knot undone: a knot in her own thread, tied by her own hand, at a time she has forgotten. It is hers, and yours to loose. The knot is also what holds a whole row of her days together.

choices.text: Loosen it, and let the row rearrange

effects.log: You loosen it. The row of days reshuffles into something she can live in.

choices.text: Leave it and tell her what it holds

effects.log: You tell her in a dream. She keeps the knot, and understands.

choices.text: Weave a second thread to carry the load

effects.log: It takes three years of your attention. The knot becomes an ornament.

events.text: Dreams are your domain, and one night you see how a dream within a dream folds neatly, like a handkerchief. You fold one, and then another, and find you do not know which dream you are standing in. It is not frightening. It is merely new.

choices.text: Walk out the outermost door

effects.log: You walk out through three doors and find a morning. It is the most real morning you have known.

choices.text: Stay a while in the middle

effects.log: You stay in the middle and listen to the sleepers of the world. It is a vast quiet murmur.

choices.text: Leave a note in the deepest dream

effects.log: You leave a note for whoever comes next. They will read it as their own thought.

events.text: A dreamer refuses to wake from the best night of their life. They have been sleeping for nine days, and their family is frightened. You hold Dreams; you could end the night with a breath. The dream, you can see, is truly lovely.

choices.text: Wake them gently

effects.log: You wake them with the smell of their own kitchen. They weep, and then eat, and then sleep like a person.

choices.text: Join the dream a moment first

effects.log: You walk in it. It is lovely, and you carry one small piece of it out.

choices.text: Let the dream finish on its own

effects.log: You leave it. On the tenth day the dream ends as dreams do, and nobody is angry.

events.text: You hold Life, and in an idle hour you hold a single seed and feel it want. Not want like a person; want like a direction. The seed is not asking you for anything. It is only pointing, and you are the only one in a hundred leagues who can see which way.

choices.text: Plant it where it points

effects.log: You plant it. A tree comes up that will be a landmark for ten thousand years.

choices.text: Study the pointing

effects.log: You sit with the seed a full season. Life is mostly a matter of direction, and you learn to read it.

choices.text: Give the seed to a mortal gardener

effects.log: You leave it on a gardener's sill. She plants it without suspicion and is astonished by the result.

events.text: An orchard in a drought is dying, and its keeper has prayed to you every morning for a year. You hold Life. The prayer is simple. The difficulty is that rain from you means a dry field elsewhere, and you can feel the whole ledger of water.

choices.text: Give rain and take it from your own domain's margin

effects.log: You pay out of your own margin. The orchard lives; the margin sulks and recovers.

choices.text: Teach the keeper to dig for the old spring

effects.log: A dream shows the old spring. It is a harder answer and a more lasting one.

choices.text: Let the orchard die and replant

effects.log: It dies. The seedlings come in the spring, and the keeper does not forgive you quite.

events.text: The wild is yours, and you have learned its great patience: the heron that stands for an hour, the cat that sits by a hole until the world changes its mind. Today you sit among them. Nobody notices a god who is being as still as the others.

choices.text: Stay a season among them

effects.log: You stay a season. When you leave, the beasts do not look up, which is the highest compliment they have.

choices.text: Teach a beast something small

effects.log: You teach a fox to open a latch. It is a mischievous kindness.

choices.text: Learn a beast's way of waiting

effects.log: You learn the heron's. It becomes a cultivation posture that sticks.

events.text: A hunter and a wolf make the same prayer on the same night: to be fed and not found. You hold Beasts. Their needs cross in a stand of birch. You could let one win and one lose; you could also, with more trouble, find a third way.

choices.text: Find the third way: a deer too old to run

effects.log: You arrange it. The hunter eats, the wolf eats, the deer was ready, and nobody is angry.

choices.text: Favour the wolf

effects.log: You favour the wolf, for it is yours. The hunter's family has a lean winter.

choices.text: Favour the hunter

effects.log: You favour the hunter, for children wait. The wolf goes hungry and watches you with a look you remember.

events.text: The Harvest is yours, and its law is plain: what is sown comes back, with the weather's interest. You sit at the end of a field at dusk and feel the whole law moving through the rows. It seems to apply to you as well, and you wonder what you have sown.

choices.text: Walk back through your last thousand years and look

effects.log: You look. The rows are crooked in places and tall in others. It is a fair harvest.

choices.text: Sow something kind on purpose

effects.log: You sow a small kindness in a stranger. You will see its return in a century, and it is a long wait.

choices.text: Ask Pungnyeon about the law's fine print

effects.log: Pungnyeon says there is none: it is all a matter of attention. You are not sure if that is comfort.

events.text: A glut has come to the fields you keep, and fruit is rotting in the rows faster than anyone can carry it away. The farmers pray to you with real anger. You hold the Harvest, and have given them too much. It is a strange sin to have committed.

choices.text: Slow the ripening

effects.log: You slow it. The harvest comes in at a pace people can lift, and nobody understands why.

choices.text: Send the surplus to a distant country

effects.log: You send a wind with the seeds on it. A hungry coast has a good year.

choices.text: Admit the mistake to the farmers in a dream

effects.log: They wake and laugh and forgive you, and they make a feast of the excess.

events.text: The Sea is yours, and its patience is endless. You spend a decade walking the bed of a bay and learn that a tide is not a pull but a long, slow agreement. Each wave is a small yes. You have not said yes to anything in a very long time.

choices.text: Practise saying yes, in small things

effects.log: You say yes to a stranger's question and a wanderer's plea. The agreement spreads through you like warmth.

choices.text: Study the long agreement

effects.log: You study it for the rest of the decade. It is a different kind of strength than holding.

choices.text: Make a gift of a sunken thing

effects.log: You raise a lost bell from the sand and leave it on a beach. A child finds it and rings it.

events.text: A sailor's widow comes down to the shore every evening and says her husband's name to the water. You hold the Sea. He is not in it, exactly; he is part of it, as every drowned thing is. She does not ask you for anything. She only says his name.

choices.text: Let a wave say it back

effects.log: A single wave returns the name in a long hush. She sits on the sand until dawn.

choices.text: Send her a dream of him laughing

effects.log: You do. She wakes with a face on her mind she had forgotten, and sleeps well for a year.

choices.text: Say nothing and keep the tide gentle

effects.log: You keep the tide low for her evenings. It is the quietest favour you have done.

events.text: Thunder is yours, and you spend an age learning that the drum before the strike matters more than the strike. The long rumble is a kind of promise, and promise is the heart of the domain. You sit in the rumble a whole night and do not let the lightning fall.

choices.text: Hold the rumble a little longer

effects.log: You hold it. The valley below waits, held in the breath, and the morning is clear.

choices.text: Let the lightning fall on empty ground

effects.log: You let it fall in an empty bog. It lights the whole sky and hurts nobody.

choices.text: Learn to sing in the rumble

effects.log: It is a deep song and nobody hears it. It carries across the sea.

events.text: A bell-ringer's child is terrified of thunder and has begun to pray against it, to you, in a whisper, every storm. You hold Thunder. The child does not know. You could make the storms quieter; you could also make yourself known.

choices.text: Quiet the storms near the child

effects.log: You turn the storms aside, one by one. The child grows up unafraid and never knows why.

choices.text: Send a dream of a friendly drum

effects.log: In the dream the child beats the thunder like a drum. They wake delighted.

choices.text: Stand at the window as the storm and be known

effects.log: You let the child see the shape of you in the lightning. They stare, and stop fearing, and start to study.

events.text: The Mountains are yours, and their stillness is not rest but an enormous act of attention. You spend a hundred years as nothing but a presence under a peak, and learn that stillness is the hardest thing a god can do. It is also the thing most worth doing.

choices.text: Be still a little longer

effects.log: You are still a little longer. The peak decides you are part of it and drops a boulder somewhere kind.

choices.text: Share the stillness with a pilgrim

effects.log: You let a pilgrim sit beside you on the summit and feel it. They go home quiet for the rest of their life.

choices.text: Move one mountain a hair

effects.log: You shift a peak by the width of a hair. It is the most daring thing you have ever done.

events.text: A village beneath a landslide-prone slope refuses to leave. The elders have prayed to you for generations to hold the mountain. You hold the Mountains, and the mountain will not be held forever. The truth of it is in the stone.

choices.text: Tell them in a dream that they must go

effects.log: They go, grieving. The slope slides a year later, and the village sleeps elsewhere.

choices.text: Hold the mountain as long as you can

effects.log: You hold it. Each year the holding gets harder, and you know the day will come.

choices.text: Help them build where the mountain agrees

effects.log: You find them a good new site and send stonemasons in dreams. The old village is kept as a shrine.

events.text: The foundation under you is still settling. Nine thousand years is the old measure for this rung, and you feel it in your breath, which has begun to wait for you: not a pain, a patience. Below the clouds a calendar turns over a whole age without noticing you sat still.

choices.text: Stand at the harbour wall until your breath returns

effects.log: The keeper lets you stay. Your breath waits, then comes in on a bell-note, and the wall hums under your hand.

choices.text: Breathe in time with the well and learn its long count

effects.log: The water in the deep well rises and falls once in a hundred breaths. You borrow its count for the foundation.

choices.text: Ask Cheonho what the Sky does with a breath held this long

effects.log: Cheonho says the Sky keeps it, and calls it weather. You laugh, and the waiting eases.

choices.text: Let the harbour bells ring you the hours

effects.log: You stop counting yourself and let the bells do it. Three seasons go by like one long exhale.

events.text: A flaw you had forgotten is setting into your foundation along with everything else: a habit of thought from a rung ago, now nine thousand years from being moved. Cheonho says it can still be turned if you take it up now, or built into the wall if you do not.

choices.text: Ring the habit out with the Bell Terrace

effects.log: You tune each bell against the flaw until its note goes flat and false. Then you know it by sound and can unlearn it.

choices.text: Ask the lighthouse keeper how a fault in a lens is lived with

effects.log: The keeper says you steer by the lamp and mind the glare. You steer around the flaw for a decade.

choices.text: Let Cheonho wind it into the Sky until it thins

effects.log: Cheonho takes the habit up and lets the wind comb it out. It comes back weaker, and then not at all.

events.text: You wake from a three-year meditation with Cheonho's lamp burning at the foot of your seat. They kept it lit the whole time and left a note: the foundation was loud in the night, and they did not want you to wake in the dark.

choices.text: Ring Cheonho a morning bell from the terrace

effects.log: One clear stroke at dawn, sent down the Bell Terrace to their door. They send back two.

choices.text: Go and keep the lighthouse lamp one night for the keeper

effects.log: The keeper sleeps. You tend a lamp that is not yours and learn what it costs to be the one awake.

choices.text: Read the note and sleep in the dark on purpose

effects.log: You blow the lamp out, lie down, and let the foundation be loud. It is only loud, and then it is quiet.

choices.text: Write them a reply and leave it at their seat

effects.log: You say thanks in four lines and sign it with a smaller hand than you use.

events.text: The gate above you is shut, and the reason is plain: it asks for a Perfect Dao, and you do not have it yet. You stand before it every few centuries, as one stands before a locked door in one's own house, and know there is nobody to shout at.

choices.text: Study the shape of a Perfect Dao in the ropes of the harbour

effects.log: The lighthouse keeper shows you a splice that has no weak point. You go home and look for yours.

choices.text: Stand at the gate and breathe, and be refused

effects.log: You wait for your breath to catch up with you. It does, and the gate is as shut as before.

choices.text: Walk the harbour wall at night and ask the Sky for a sign

effects.log: Cheonho lights one star above the wall. It does not say anything. It is enough.

events.text: Cheonho is certain your Dao is deep enough for what is next. The gate disagrees, and the gate has read it more carefully than anyone. It asks for a Perfect Dao, and a friend's confidence is not on the list.

choices.text: Ask Cheonho to try your Dao against the winter wind

effects.log: They lead you to the roof of the Sky and let the wind try you. It finds a draught in your third gate.

choices.text: Thank Cheonho and ring a bell for their faith

effects.log: The sound runs the length of the terrace. They are embarrassed and stand a little straighter.

choices.text: Let the lighthouse keeper ask you plain questions about your Dao

effects.log: She asks if you can see in fog. You find that you cannot, and begin to learn.

events.text: A mortal scholar's prayer asks why a god cannot simply walk through a gate they are strong enough for. You read it twice. The honest answer is that the gate asks for a Perfect Dao, not strength, and you are still turning the difference over.

choices.text: Answer on the harbour bells in a pattern only the scholar knows

effects.log: They hear it and write the pattern into a treatise. Sailors hum it for years.

choices.text: Keep the prayer on the terrace where the wind can read it

effects.log: The wind reads it a hundred times. Each time the question looks smaller and truer.

choices.text: Send the scholar the lighthouse keeper as a teacher

effects.log: The keeper tells them about locks and keys over three long evenings. The scholar goes home content.

choices.text: Pass it to the Court of Ministries

effects.log: It is filed under Questions Unsuited to Gods. A clerk annotates it: Excellent. Unanswerable.

events.text: Cheonho tells you, over tea nobody drinks, about the time the gate above this rung turned them back. They went in sure and came out with their sleeves smoking. The lesson was a small one, they say, and took four hundred years to understand.

choices.text: Ask Cheonho whether the bells rang when they were turned back

effects.log: They say all of them rang, in the wrong order. You write the right order beside it.

choices.text: Ask what the wind said on the way back

effects.log: Cheonho says it said nothing, and that was the lesson: nobody was lying to them.

choices.text: Say you will not fail it, quietly, only to yourself

effects.log: You promise yourself, not them. Cheonho sees the promise and lets it stand.

choices.text: Offer to go up with them next time as a second pair of hands

effects.log: Cheonho is touched past speaking. You agree to wait for the next opening.

events.text: You hear that a god one rung above you tried the gate after it and failed. The Silent Hall will not say how. A candle is lit for them in a mountain temple ringed with bells, and the whole pantheon is careful not to look at the candle.

choices.text: Ring the terrace bell once, for them, and keep the echo

effects.log: It travels down the Sky and does not come back. You keep what it carried.

choices.text: Read the map of the cliff drawn by someone who fell

effects.log: You study each handhold. The fourth is a lie, and the fall begins there.

choices.text: Ask the harbour keeper whether a lamp can be lit for the lost

effects.log: She hangs one on the wall in the lee. It burns all season, and no ship is lost under it.

events.text: You find a record in the Hall of old ascents: a god's account of their own failure at this gate, written for no one. The last page says they stopped trying and simply taught for a thousand years. It reads as if it were the best outcome they could imagine.

choices.text: Copy it out and ring the Bell Terrace once for them

effects.log: The ring carries across the sea. A faint bell answers from the other side of the harbour.

choices.text: Seek the old god and ask what the wind taught them

effects.log: They say the wind taught them to stop pushing. Their school is at the top of a hundred steps.

choices.text: Return the record and keep the gate in view

effects.log: You put it back and look at the gate with fresh eyes. It looks less like a wall and more like a door.

choices.text: Read it to the lighthouse keeper on a foggy night

effects.log: She says she has taught ten thousand ships and never been less than glad of it. You notice.

events.text: The night before you try the gate, the world is odd. The harbour bells ring without wind. Your foundation is the shape of a held breath. You wonder, for the first time in ages, what you would regret not having said to someone.

choices.text: Ring one bell in the dark, softly, for whoever hears

effects.log: The harbour wakes a little and goes back to sleep. Someone far off rings back.

choices.text: Tell the lighthouse keeper what you would have said

effects.log: She listens without turning the lamp. When you finish she says, "Go to bed, they heard you."

choices.text: Walk the harbour wall until the bells stop on their own

effects.log: They stop at dawn, one by one. You arrive at the gate with an empty head and a full chest.

choices.text: Write the regret on a strip of paper and tie it to a bell-rope

effects.log: The rope carries it up into the dark. In the morning it is gone.

events.text: On the eve of the gate, Cheonho appears at your door with a sealed jar and no explanation. The jar holds an old breeze. "For afterwards," they say, "if you want to remember what it was like to be only this."

choices.text: Take it and tie it to a bell-rope

effects.log: The jar rings faintly whenever the bell does. Cheonho smiles each time.

choices.text: Open it on the terrace and let it out among the bells

effects.log: Every bell sounds once. The old breeze joins the Sky and the knot in your chest loosens.

choices.text: Ask Cheonho to tell you what the breeze was before it was kept

effects.log: They say it was a morning at sea. You make them tell it twice.

choices.text: Decline kindly; you will not look back from the stair

effects.log: They nod and take the jar. You go on up the stairs without turning.

events.text: A tally of the nine thousand years behind you is the oddest comfort. You list what you learned at each rung, and notice that the best things were not what you were chasing. Tomorrow you try the gate. Tonight you finish the list.

choices.text: Read the list from the terrace and let the wind correct it

effects.log: The wind takes a page and returns it with the margins rearranged. It reads better.

choices.text: Read it aloud to the lighthouse keeper

effects.log: She hears it as one hears a shipping forecast, and says: fair weather ahead. You believe her.

choices.text: Give the list to a young god of the Sky

effects.log: They take it up the stairs with both hands. Cheonho watches them go.

choices.text: Cut the list down to one line

effects.log: You keep: be kind, mostly. It is short enough to remember at the gate.

events.text: Cheonho taps a place under the left collarbone and says there is a hairline in the foundation there. Not a danger, but a place where weather will one day find a way in. It sits in the exact spot where you were proudest.

choices.text: Have the bells rung against the flaw until it sings a true note

effects.log: Cheonho conducts. The hairline hums, and then does not, and you no longer need to be proud there.

choices.text: Seal it with salt-wind from the harbour

effects.log: You rub it with sea-air a season. The flaw closes into a pale scar.

choices.text: Tell Cheonho you were proud of that spot

effects.log: It is a hard thing to say. They say they were proud of it too, and then the spot cools between you.

choices.text: Study the weather that finds the hairline

effects.log: You watch each gust enter and leave. It is a small, exact map of how you are loved and tested.

events.text: A hollow in your divine foundation shows up only on feast days, when the faithful of a harbour wall press too close. Your power swells and a little of you thins at the edges, like paper held to a lamp. You do not quite recognize your own voice at the end of the day.

choices.text: Stand at the end of the harbour wall and let them come to you in ones

effects.log: They come in small groups across the stones. The hollow stays closed.

choices.text: Have the bells ring the crowd in at a slower pace

effects.log: Bell by bell they enter the harbour, and you feel each as a single weight.

choices.text: Hold the feast at the lighthouse and let the keeper count them in

effects.log: She counts them, name by name, as they climb. The hollow stays shut.

choices.text: Go thin on purpose, and watch where the thinness ends

effects.log: You find your edge at a surprising distance. It was further than you thought.

events.text: You found a flaw in the way you hold your Dao: it leans toward a sea, and away from the small things that live in it. A divine foundation can tilt for ten thousand years without cracking, and be wrong the whole time.

choices.text: Come down to the harbour wall and count its stones

effects.log: There are four thousand and one. You know the third one now by name.

choices.text: Look through the lighthouse keeper's eyes for one night

effects.log: She sees every ship's small lamp. You see the Sky differently after.

choices.text: Learn the smallest bell on the terrace

effects.log: Cheonho shows you the tiny one the children ring. It teaches you proportion.

choices.text: Tilt on purpose toward the sea, then back

effects.log: You oscillate for a season. The swing teaches you where your middle is.

events.text: You can feel a whole sea coast of the devout in the cool quiet of your work: not as sound, but as pressure, like deep water. Today a prayer comes up through it that is more tender than most, and your qi leaps in answer before you have chosen to hear.

choices.text: Answer with a clear bell-note over their rooftop

effects.log: One pure tone, no wind. They hear it, and the qi in you rings once and rests.

choices.text: Let the prayer rise on through you into the Sky

effects.log: It goes up the stairs of the bells and out. You are lighter after.

choices.text: Trace the prayer to its harbour and sit by its author unseen

effects.log: A fisher mends a net and prays under their breath. You stay till the net is done.

choices.text: Take the lift and climb with it, one stair

effects.log: You use the swell for one step toward the gate. You feel their hands under you and are careful.

events.text: A famine has driven everyone around a harbour wall to your name, and the prayers are the loudest you have ever heard. Faith like that is a rare strength. It is also the strength of people who have nothing left to spend, and you know what it costs them.

choices.text: Take a little and answer with fog and sea-fish for the harbour

effects.log: The nets fill. The strength you took is repaid in herring.

choices.text: Refuse the strength and ring the bells to call help from the coast

effects.log: Ships turn in from three coasts. You owe the harbour a debt you are glad to carry.

choices.text: Drink it fully; the bell's rule is the faithful

effects.log: You take it all. The harbour is silent after, and you hear the silence in your own bell.

choices.text: Ask the lighthouse keeper what she has seen in worse years

effects.log: She tells you of a winter when a lamp was kept lit through a whole famine. You keep that lamp lit again.

events.text: The faithful have taught you by accident. The prayer of a lighthouse keeper, long and dull and sincere, moves your qi more than a dazzling one. It is the repetition that does it, like a sea against a rock, and you have been waiting for lightning when you should have loved the tide.

choices.text: Listen to the lighthouse keeper's nightly murmur, all of it

effects.log: It is the same list every night. You sleep like a lamp: steady, patient.

choices.text: Ring the plain prayers on a bell of their own

effects.log: Cheonho has one cast. The terrace now has a bell for the dull and sincere.

choices.text: Compare the dull prayers with the dazzling ones, side by side

effects.log: The dull ones last longer. You note it carefully.

choices.text: Keep it as your own craft, shared with no one

effects.log: You tell nobody. You do grow, and quietly.

events.text: Your people have built you a mountain temple ringed with bells. They hang offerings on its rail every dawn, not grand ones: a knotted rope, a child's drawing of you with too many arms. The offerings do something for your qi, and something else for your temper.

choices.text: Let a bell ring on the rail when the child hangs their drawing

effects.log: It rings once, softly. The child looks up and decides to draw you again.

choices.text: Keep the knotted rope and unpick the knots, one by one, in thanks

effects.log: Each knot is a wish. You answer three and leave the rest as a prayer-bed.

choices.text: Receive the offerings in silence, and let the qi settle

effects.log: The rail grows full. The mountain wind feels warmer.

choices.text: Ask the temple to pull the oldest offerings down for the poor

effects.log: They do. The rail is lighter and the poor are a bit warmer.

events.text: The keeper of a mountain temple ringed with bells has quietly become rich on your name, and the offerings now go through three hands before they reach the altar. You can feel the thinning in your qi. The priest is old, kind to their neighbours and, you think, afraid.

choices.text: Ring the temple bells off-key until the priest listens

effects.log: He hears the discord all week. On the seventh day he opens the ledger.

choices.text: Send the lighthouse keeper to pray quietly beside the altar

effects.log: Her honest murmur works on the priest like a draught. He amends his ways.

choices.text: Mind the thin qi and say nothing, and watch

effects.log: You observe for a decade. The priest dies kind and quiet, and his successor is honest.

choices.text: Let it go; the faith is the faith

effects.log: You stay silent. The offerings come as ever, and a little shame comes with them.

events.text: On your festival day, at a mountain temple ringed with bells, a family of strangers leaves no offering at all. They simply sit on the steps and eat, and talk, and let a child nap with her head on a worn stone. Your qi rises more from that than from the heaped altar.

choices.text: Let the bells rest for the evening

effects.log: The terrace falls silent. The nap runs long and the family goes home rested.

choices.text: Ask the wardens to dim the lanterns, gently

effects.log: They do. The family sits in dusk and no one stares.

choices.text: Study how a ring of bells makes a place feel guarded

effects.log: You hear the shape of silence between strokes. It is a lesson in rest.

choices.text: Join them, unseen, on the bottom step

effects.log: You sit beside the child. She stirs and murmurs a name that might be yours.

events.text: Your domain stretches now across a sea, and a small thing in it happens only because you let it: a late frost holds off, a river changes its mind. You are discovering that a god's power is mostly a list of things they decline to do.

choices.text: Decline one more gale, and mark it on the harbour chart

effects.log: The chart gains a line. Ships come home on a morning that had planned to be rough.

choices.text: Reach for a small act: part one cloud over the wall

effects.log: The cloud parts and a beam falls on the lighthouse. The keeper looks up and smiles.

choices.text: Walk the coast and ask each cape what is owed

effects.log: The capes list their debts. A sea-wall wants mending, a spring wants naming.

events.text: Two of your domain's laws have begun to disagree. The same rain that feeds a field drowns a village below it, and you are the only one who can say which matters more. Cheonho has offered to hold one of the laws for you while you think.

choices.text: Accept Cheonho's offer to hold the law of rain, and think a hundred years

effects.log: They hold it in a high pocket of Sky. You think. The answer is not the one you came with.

choices.text: Decide at once for the harbour, and bear what follows

effects.log: You choose. The village below is moved to higher ground, and you attend every wedding.

choices.text: Give the question to the lighthouse keeper and the villagers together

effects.log: They rig a series of dikes with lamps for markers. It beats your answer.

events.text: A god of the green assembly asks to see how you keep your domain. They stay a month, taking notes, asking questions, never praising. On the last day they say your domain is the least beautiful they have seen, and the most alive.

choices.text: Thank them; the least beautiful and most alive is the praise

effects.log: They go home with a sheaf of notes about a sea they have never seen.

choices.text: Ask what they would change in your Sky

effects.log: They name three things. You change two, and the third, which hurts, you keep.

choices.text: Return the visit and be unpraised in their Green Assembly

effects.log: You spend a month among their trees. It is humbling and the soil is excellent.

events.text: A Revelation arrives over a harbour wall the way weather arrives: not as words, but a rearrangement of the air. You spend a month deciphering it and are left with one phrase you cannot stop turning over, like a stone in the mouth. It seems to be about patience.

choices.text: Ring the phrase out on a single bell until it opens

effects.log: The bell gives back a different phrase. The two together make a sentence.

choices.text: Read it to the harbour keeper and take her puzzled silence

effects.log: She says it sounds like a weather report from a country that has not been born. You treasure it.

choices.text: Keep it in the sea-air and ask no more

effects.log: It travels the harbour for a year. You are left with a feeling, not a meaning, and are content.

events.text: A manual of the gods has come into your keeping, copied seven times over by seven tired hands. In the margin of the fourth chapter, someone has written in a different ink: "This does not work near the water in a deep well." You are not sure if that is a warning or a joke.

choices.text: Try the chapter in the shadow of a well and see why it fails

effects.log: The well says no in its own voice. You write that down.

choices.text: Ask Cheonho who might have written the note

effects.log: Cheonho says: someone who hated wells. A good lead, a long search.

choices.text: Write your own note beside it: "Try it from a rooftop"

effects.log: It sits there for ages. A young god tries it, and is glad.

events.text: In the night a Revelation comes that is not for you. It is meant for a young god of the Sky, and has simply fallen on the wrong roof, here beside a harbour wall. It is lovely, and it will do you a little good, and it is not yours.

choices.text: Ring the young god of the Sky down from the terrace and hand it over on the stair

effects.log: The bell tolls once and they come down bewildered to receive it.

choices.text: Let the harbour wind carry it to them unread

effects.log: The wind delivers it into their lap. You never know if it was welcome.

choices.text: Keep it for one night by the lighthouse lamp, then return it

effects.log: It does you a little good. You return it with a bell as apology.

choices.text: Keep it, and be grateful quietly

effects.log: It helps you. You will not look at the harbour wall for a decade.

events.text: A clerk of the Heavenly Court asks you to confirm a line in the Book of Fates: a lighthouse keeper is to die in their sleep, tonight, at forty. It is a small, ordinary line. You are not required to object. The ink is not quite dry.

choices.text: Confirm it, and ring the harbour bell once at the hour

effects.log: The bell tolls once. The keeper looks up from her lamp and knows, and tends it all the same.

choices.text: Ask the clerk whether a death at sea could be a death at home

effects.log: He can change the place and not the hour. You choose her own bed over the water.

choices.text: Decline, and sit the night out beside the lighthouse stair

effects.log: The Book frowns and holds. She sleeps on and wakes in the morning to find you gone.

choices.text: Take the day to learn who will miss her

effects.log: You learn the names of six ships. You bring that to the clerk, who nods.

events.text: You are called as a witness before a Judge of Souls. A lighthouse keeper you once answered with a small mercy stands accused of selling short measure at a harbour wall. Your testimony will not decide, but it will weigh. The Judge asks nothing but "What did you see?" and waits.

choices.text: Tell exactly what you saw at the harbour wall

effects.log: The tide table, the weights, the day. The Judge writes and the matter closes.

choices.text: Add the lighthouse keeper as a second witness

effects.log: She is blunt and exact. The matter ends sooner.

choices.text: Tell it kindly, with a longer harbour-day than there was

effects.log: You stretch it by a breath. The Judge writes nothing.

choices.text: Decline: you do not weigh a stranger's rope

effects.log: The Judge accepts it. You walk out through the wind lighter and a little ashamed.

events.text: The Court's archivist gives you a rare gift: an hour alone with the Book of Fates, open at your own page. It is blank except for a single line in a small neat hand: "Not yet written." You find that this is the most comforting sentence you have read.

choices.text: Close the Book, and ring the Bell Terrace once for the unwritten

effects.log: The bell is for what is not written yet. It carries a long way.

choices.text: Write a line, and let the wind take the page

effects.log: The page flies into the Sky. You never see it again, and are relieved.

choices.text: Ask the archivist whether the Book can be read aloud to a ship

effects.log: The archivist laughs and says: only to a very patient one.

choices.text: Read the neat hand again and trace its stroke

effects.log: It is Cheonho's hand. You do not tell them.

events.text: You spend a century with the water in a deep well, the nearest thing to what your Dao answers: you let it slip through your fingers, you taste it, you let it carry you. You discover that the Dao is not the element, but the way the element refuses to be held.

choices.text: Lower yourself into the deep well and let the water push you up

effects.log: It refuses you, gently, one metre at a time. You rise holding nothing.

choices.text: Cup water in the harbour and watch it keep its shape for a breath

effects.log: A moment, then gone. Cupping is a courtesy.

choices.text: Ask the water what it remembers of the sky

effects.log: It answers with a single raindrop. It is enough.

events.text: You have watched the water in a deep well a million times, and today it looks different. It is nothing. It is the same element at a new angle. Your Dao takes a half-step and you are very careful not to move.

choices.text: Hold still while the well-water tilts

effects.log: The surface tilts and a face you do not know looks up at you. It is yours.

choices.text: Follow the new angle down the well

effects.log: You follow it to the bottom, where a coin lies. You keep the coin.

choices.text: Draw the water up and see if it looks the same in a cup

effects.log: It does not. You pour it out slowly and watch the angle go.

choices.text: Tell the lighthouse keeper what you saw

effects.log: She says she has seen it in fog. She draws it for you.

events.text: A child at a harbour wall is playing with the water in a deep well, not knowing it. They are doing it badly and joyfully, and a thing you spent a thousand years learning falls out of their hands by accident. You are not sure whether to be annoyed.

choices.text: Watch the child drop pebbles into the harbour well

effects.log: The ripples teach you something about the water's memory. You steal the ripples.

choices.text: Send a dream of a kind boatman to teach her to row

effects.log: She rows well by ten. She never knows who taught her.

choices.text: Stay away; wells are for children and secrets

effects.log: You leave the child to the water. Some joys need privacy.

choices.text: Ask the lighthouse keeper whether the child may keep the lamp one night

effects.log: She lets her. The child sleeps by it, proud and alone.

events.text: You are asked to give the opening address at a council of pantheons in the Bell Terrace: a short talk on what a god owes the faithful. The Will of Heaven says order, the Silent Hall says remembrance, the Green Assembly says growth, the Throne of Storms says weight. You must pick, or find a fifth.

choices.text: Say a god owes a clear signal, and have the Bell Terrace ring it

effects.log: One note, no echo. The Will of Heaven nods; the Throne of Storms grumbles in tune.

choices.text: Say a god owes remembrance of the ships that did not return

effects.log: The Silent Hall inclines. Cheonho lights a candle for the drowned.

choices.text: Say a god owes the faithful a lighthouse and nothing grander

effects.log: The Green Assembly laughs, then does not. A lamp appears on the table.

choices.text: Propose a fifth: a god owes a place to turn back

effects.log: The council argues four hours. The fifth is adopted as a footnote.

events.text: A doctrine you have followed for ages turns out, on a close reading, to be a mistranslation: one word (ring) was swapped by a scribe, and an entire school of devotion built on the swap. The error is beautiful. Correcting it would cost a lot of people their favourite prayer.

choices.text: Ring the correction across the terrace in one long peal

effects.log: The faithful hear it and weep; the new prayer is plainer and better.

choices.text: Add a footnote in the margin of the bell-book

effects.log: A modest footnote. The bell-ringers learn two versions and ring both.

choices.text: Ask the sea-faithful how they pray it, and follow them

effects.log: They had already corrected it by ear. You publish what they use.

choices.text: Keep it quiet; the prayer is doing good

effects.log: You say nothing. Every dawn the harbour sings the swapped word, and you flinch.

events.text: In the Bell Terrace, a god of the Green Assembly asks you to explain your doctrine without using any of its words. You try and fail. You try again and succeed halfway. By the end you have learned what you actually believe, which is smaller and truer than the doctrine.

choices.text: Thank them and rewrite your teaching in bell-strokes alone

effects.log: The strokes need no words. Half your students leave; the rest hear.

choices.text: Admit that the doctrine is a bell and the bell is not the sound

effects.log: They smile; the Bell Terrace rings once without anyone touching it.

choices.text: Defend the doctrine elegantly, out of habit

effects.log: You do. They nod and go; the Sky feels thinner.

choices.text: Ask them to explain theirs without its words in turn

effects.log: They try, and fail, and laugh. You both feel better.

events.text: You catch yourself at the old etiquette again: never turning your back on a stair. It is a habit from your Upper Realm centuries, and the gods in the Bell Terrace are politely baffled. A cup is just a cup here.

choices.text: Turn your back on a stair on purpose, and laugh when nothing happens

effects.log: The stair does not mind. The Bell Terrace is amused.

choices.text: Keep the habit; it makes you a careful god

effects.log: A bell-ringer copies it. It becomes a custom with a slight bow.

choices.text: Ask Cheonho what the stair meant in the Upper Realm

effects.log: They tell you, and it was a worse story than you remembered.

choices.text: Thank the stair and walk it facing the sea

effects.log: You walk it backward, facing the harbour. It is a delight.

events.text: You still keep a ledger of favours owed, a leftover of the immortals' exchange. The oldest line is a night of shelter. A god would never keep one, and when a friend sees it they look briefly hurt. The ledger is accurate to the grain, and entirely beside the point.

choices.text: Ring the ledger out aloud, a favour at a time, and forgive each

effects.log: It takes a whole morning. The bells enjoy it.

choices.text: Keep the ledger but forget where you put it

effects.log: It is found by a sweeper. She returns it, reading nothing.

choices.text: Write what you now owe, and deliver it by bell-rope

effects.log: Each debt lands on a doorstep. The sum is humbling.

choices.text: Ask the night of shelter's giver how much it was worth to them

effects.log: They say: nothing. You learn something about price.

events.text: You flinched at a bell today. The Upper Realm taught you to expect a hand behind such things, and the habit lives in the shoulders long after the cause is gone. Here nothing is behind them, and your body has not yet been told.

choices.text: Stand beneath the Bell Terrace at full peal and keep still

effects.log: The sound passes through you. Your shoulders drop.

choices.text: Ring the bell yourself, again and again, until it cannot startle you

effects.log: By the hundredth stroke you hum along.

choices.text: Ask a god born here how a bell was ever a friend

effects.log: They never knew otherwise. You envy them for an hour.

choices.text: Walk the stair with your back to the drop

effects.log: Nothing is behind you but the sea. Your shoulders drop.

events.text: A lighthouse keeper prays, in a harbour wall, with a coil of rope in their other hand. They do not ask for anything. They only say "thank you for the weather." You, who keep weather, find that nobody has ever thanked you for it before.

choices.text: Clear the fog off the harbour for the keeper's morning

effects.log: She looks out and the whole bay is bright. She coils her rope in good spirits.

choices.text: Keep the thanks by you, folded small, where the wind cannot take it

effects.log: You carry it for a century. It makes your gales gentler.

choices.text: Ask what she would change, by dream

effects.log: She says: nothing, but a little less fog on Sundays. You oblige.

choices.text: Send the first gull of the day to sit on her wall

effects.log: The gull stays. She names it.

events.text: A prayer reaches you from a lighthouse keeper who has never believed in gods. "If you are there, I do not need you to do anything. I only wanted to say it out loud, to someone." It is the most honest prayer you have heard in a century.

choices.text: Answer nothing and let the harbour bells murmur until she sleeps

effects.log: They murmur low, then silent. She sleeps.

choices.text: Send a quiet sign: one bell, once, no wind

effects.log: She hears it and does not ask why.

choices.text: Ask your pantheon what this is called

effects.log: They have no word. You name it: the listening-prayer.

choices.text: Ask the lighthouse keeper whether she has ever prayed like this

effects.log: She says: every night, for forty years, to the lamp. You blink.

events.text: A mother prays that her child's cold fever might ease, and the prayer is wrong in an instructive way: she asks the wrong god, for the wrong thing, and misspells your name. It reaches you anyway, because the love in it knows the way. You stay with the wrongness of the address.

choices.text: Ease the cold fever yourself, quietly, and leave a warm blanket

effects.log: She thanks the wrong god, and the child sleeps.

choices.text: Ring the prayer on to the god of Healing by bell

effects.log: He hears it and complains. The mother gets a tincture.

choices.text: Learn from how love finds the address through fog

effects.log: You follow it as a ship follows a lamp. It is a map.

choices.text: Appear in the mother's dream as the right god, kindly

effects.log: She wakes and thanks the right name, and the fever breaks.

events.text: The foundation under you is still settling. Ten thousand years is the old measure for this rung, and you feel it in your hands, which stay exactly where you put them: not a pain, a patience. Below the clouds a calendar turns over a whole age without noticing you sat still.

choices.text: Keep your hands exactly where you put them

effects.log: You set them on your knees and leave them a decade. The still hands teach the whole foundation how to rest.

choices.text: Copy one page slowly in the scriptorium, hands full of ink

effects.log: The copyist lets you take the next desk. The slow nib steadies hands that had forgotten how to be busy.

choices.text: Weigh the stillness against what Baekun carries

effects.log: Baekun lays a small stone in your open palm. It is lighter than you feared, and you keep it.

events.text: A flaw you had forgotten is setting into your foundation along with everything else: a habit of thought from a rung ago, now ten thousand years from being moved. Baekun says it can still be turned if you take it up now, or built into the wall if you do not.

choices.text: Weigh it against the whole of your old rung and see if it deserves a place

effects.log: It does not. You write its verdict in the Pale Gallery ledger and the seam closes.

choices.text: Copy it out in a clean hand and file it away

effects.log: The copyist shows you how to turn a fault into a footnote. Written down, it stops steering you.

choices.text: Let Baekun take it as a small death

effects.log: Baekun lays the habit to rest with courtesy and a thin white cloth. You miss it for a week.

events.text: You wake from a three-year meditation with Baekun's lamp burning at the foot of your seat. They kept it lit the whole time and left a note: the foundation was loud in the night, and they did not want you to wake in the dark.

choices.text: Return the favour by copying out their old scroll

effects.log: Baekun had abandoned half of it. You finish the half in their own hand, and leave it on their desk.

choices.text: Sit up with the lamp and ask it nothing

effects.log: You keep it company through the night. The Pale Gallery is very quiet, and kindly so.

choices.text: Tell Baekun you were afraid of the dark

effects.log: It is the first thing you have admitted in an age. Baekun only nods and refills the oil.

events.text: The gate above you is shut, and the reason is plain: it asks for a second Dao at Insight, and you do not have it yet. You stand before it every few centuries, as one stands before a locked door in one's own house, and know there is nobody to shout at.

choices.text: Open a second Dao and see how thin it is

effects.log: You pull a second Dao out into the gallery light. It is wan and young. You give it a place by the window.

choices.text: Ask the copyist how one writes in two scripts at once

effects.log: She says you learn one so well it carries the other. You take that as an assignment.

choices.text: Accept the gate's refusal and go back to the first Dao

effects.log: You turn home and deepen the first Dao. The second can wait, and so can you.

events.text: Baekun is certain your Dao is deep enough for what is next. The gate disagrees, and the gate has read it more carefully than anyone. It asks for a second Dao at Insight, and a friend's confidence is not on the list.

choices.text: Hear the friend out, then correct their figures

effects.log: You show Baekun where their reckoning of your Dao is generous. It is the kindest argument you have had.

choices.text: Ask the copyist to set out the gate's demand in her own words

effects.log: She restates it in four lines. It is clearer, and more demanding.

choices.text: Go on as if nothing has been said

effects.log: You keep to your work. The friend keeps to their faith. Both are patient.

events.text: A mortal scholar's prayer asks why a god cannot simply walk through a gate they are strong enough for. You read it twice. The honest answer is that the gate asks for a second Dao at Insight, not strength, and you are still turning the difference over.

choices.text: Answer in a dream-scroll the scholar has to unroll slowly

effects.log: It unrolls one line a night for a year. By the last line they have answered it themselves.

choices.text: Have the copyist reply in her own careful hand

effects.log: She writes to the scholar as one scribe to another. Their letters go on for twenty years.

choices.text: Read the prayer aloud to Baekun and wait for their dry answer

effects.log: Baekun says the scholar is right and you are right, and that death is the only gate that opens for everyone. You frown, then nod.

events.text: Baekun tells you, over tea nobody drinks, about the time the gate above this rung turned them back. They went in sure and came out with their sleeves smoking. The lesson was a small one, they say, and took four hundred years to understand.

choices.text: Ask what Baekun would say to the one who goes after them

effects.log: Baekun thinks and says: "Bring something dry to sit on." It is the best advice you have had.

choices.text: Ask them to read you what they wrote of the failure

effects.log: They fetch a thin ledger. It is more honest than most books, and you read it twice.

choices.text: Say that you will not fail it, and mean it

effects.log: Baekun does not warn you. They only straighten your sleeve before you go.

events.text: You hear that a god one rung above you tried the gate after it and failed. The Silent Hall will not say how. A candle is lit for them in a thousand temples sharing one lamp, and the whole pantheon is careful not to look at the candle.

choices.text: Sit with the candle, and say the name aloud

effects.log: The Pale Gallery goes still. You say it three times and the third time is easy.

choices.text: Ask Baekun what they saw when the god fell

effects.log: Baekun says: a very ordinary morning. You decide that is the worst of it.

choices.text: Ask the copyist to copy out the account for the gallery

effects.log: She does, and omits the pity. The record is better for it.

events.text: You find a record in the Hall of old ascents: a god's account of their own failure at this gate, written for no one. The last page says they stopped trying and simply taught for a thousand years. It reads as if it were the best outcome they could imagine.

choices.text: Copy the last page by hand and let the ink dry for a decade

effects.log: The ink dries slowly in the Pale Gallery. Every year you read it again and it changes.

choices.text: Look for the god's students and ask what they remember

effects.log: They remember the tea. You come away with a recipe and a new idea of success.

choices.text: Put it back; the climb is not done with you

effects.log: You return it to its shelf. The gate is closer than it was.

events.text: The night before you try the gate, the world is odd. Every clock in the Hall stops at once. Your foundation is the shape of a held breath. You wonder, for the first time in ages, what you would regret not having said to someone.

choices.text: Stop every clock in the Pale Gallery on purpose, and sit

effects.log: You stop the rest too, and the Hall is quieter than death. You sleep inside it.

choices.text: Tell Baekun the regret, and let them keep it

effects.log: They write nothing down. You will never hear it from them, which is what you wanted.

choices.text: Copy the note you would have written and burn the copy

effects.log: The copyist lends you a clean sheet and a candle. You leave with an empty hand and a clear head.

events.text: On the eve of the gate, Baekun appears at your door with a sealed jar and no explanation. The jar holds an old breeze. "For afterwards," they say, "if you want to remember what it was like to be only this."

choices.text: Take the jar and put it with the stopped clocks

effects.log: It sits among them in the Pale Gallery, the only moving thing in the room.

choices.text: Let it out over the ink-stone and see what it writes

effects.log: The breeze blows a single letter across the page. You cannot read it, but you keep it.

choices.text: Decline; you will not be sentimental on this night

effects.log: Baekun takes the jar. They say sentiment is the last courtesy of the dead, and leave.

events.text: A tally of the ten thousand years behind you is the oddest comfort. You list what you learned at each rung, and notice that the best things were not what you were chasing. Tomorrow you try the gate. Tonight you finish the list.

choices.text: Read the list into the Pale Gallery's quiet

effects.log: The room takes it in. The silence after has weight, and you are grateful for it.

choices.text: Hand the list to the copyist to fair-copy

effects.log: She returns it clean, a day later, with one correction and no comment. It is the correct one.

choices.text: Give the list to Baekun to keep until after

effects.log: They file it with the dead. It is as safe as anything gets.

events.text: Baekun taps a place in the palm of your hand and says there is a hairline in the foundation there. Not a danger, but a place where weather will one day find a way in. It sits in the exact spot where you were proudest.

choices.text: Cover the hairline with a page of silence and let it set

effects.log: You press quiet over it for a year. The crack knits like a scar.

choices.text: Ask Baekun whether endings always start as hairlines

effects.log: Baekun says yes, and that most endings are also kind. You leave the crack alone.

choices.text: Have the copyist write its history in the margin

effects.log: She notes the date, the weather, the cause. The flaw becomes a fact, and facts are manageable.

events.text: A hollow in your divine foundation shows up only on feast days, when the faithful of a scriptorium press too close. Your power swells and a little of you thins at the edges, like paper held to a lamp. You do not quite recognize your own voice at the end of the day.

choices.text: Hold the rites in the Pale Gallery with only the old faithful

effects.log: A hundred people sit in silence. The hollow does not wake.

choices.text: Learn where you thin by letting the copyist chart it

effects.log: She records each swell and fade for a decade. The graph is a map of your tenderness.

choices.text: Let the feast thin you and note what the thinning leaves

effects.log: You stay. The remainder is dense and quiet, like a stone in a fast stream.

events.text: You found a flaw in the way you hold your Dao: it leans toward a continent's seasons, and away from the small things that live in it. A divine foundation can tilt for ten thousand years without cracking, and be wrong the whole time.

choices.text: Spend a week in the scriptorium copying small hands

effects.log: You copy lists, receipts, a child's alphabet. Your Dao picks up each stroke.

choices.text: Ask Baekun about the last small thing they took

effects.log: Baekun says: a spoon. They tell you its whole life. You see the lean.

choices.text: Correct it by caring for one specific dying plant

effects.log: It lives. Your Dao leans, ever so slightly, toward things that need you.

events.text: You can feel a continent that says your name at its thresholds in the cool quiet of your work: not as sound, but as pressure, like deep water. Today a prayer comes up through it that is more tender than most, and your qi leaps in answer before you have chosen to hear.

choices.text: Answer with a pause, the kind the dead take at a door

effects.log: They feel a hush in the room. They stop weeping and breathe.

choices.text: Let it pass through to the one it mourns

effects.log: The prayer reaches the departed, who were waiting. You are only a corridor.

choices.text: Copy the prayer down for the scriptorium

effects.log: It becomes a model of its kind. Others will study it for ages.

events.text: A famine has driven everyone around a scriptorium to your name, and the prayers are the loudest you have ever heard. Faith like that is a rare strength. It is also the strength of people who have nothing left to spend, and you know what it costs them.

choices.text: Take a little and send the dead's share of grain back to the living

effects.log: You open the dead's granaries in dreams. The living do not know why their cupboards are full.

choices.text: Refuse the strength and sit with the dying in the gallery of the poor

effects.log: You stay in the hall with them. Few die alone that week.

choices.text: Drink it fully; death is certain and this faith is real

effects.log: The power is vast and bitter. Baekun watches you and does not pass judgment.

events.text: The faithful have taught you by accident. The prayer of a copyist, long and dull and sincere, moves your qi more than a dazzling one. It is the repetition that does it, like a sea against a rock, and you have been waiting for lightning when you should have loved the tide.

choices.text: Sit with the copyist's prayer: the same sentence a thousand times

effects.log: It is the plainest thing you have heard. It is also the one that holds.

choices.text: Pass the practice to the Silent Hall for the roll of prayers

effects.log: Baekun adds it to their register. The Hall grows slightly gentler.

choices.text: Keep it private; some craft is a kind of mourning

effects.log: You say nothing. It feels right, and lonely.

events.text: Your people have built you a thousand temples sharing one lamp. They hang offerings on its rail every dawn, not grand ones: a folded poem, a child's drawing of you with too many arms. The offerings do something for your qi, and something else for your temper.

choices.text: Receive the folded poem and answer it with one line

effects.log: You send a line in a dream. The poet carries it for forty years in a pocket.

choices.text: Take the offerings without thanking, as the dead do

effects.log: You are not thanked either. The exchange is clean and strange.

choices.text: Ask the thousand temples to share the one lamp more evenly

effects.log: They do. A different temple is bright each night, and the rail is happier.

events.text: The keeper of a thousand temples sharing one lamp has quietly become rich on your name, and the offerings now go through three hands before they reach the altar. You can feel the thinning in your qi. The priest is old, kind to their neighbours and, you think, afraid.

choices.text: Visit the priest in a dream with the copyist's ledger

effects.log: You show him an honest page. He sees himself in it and sets about copying a better one.

choices.text: Send an auditor of the Court into the temple

effects.log: The books are straightened out within the season. Everyone is relieved and nobody is happy.

choices.text: Say nothing; the dead are patient with thieves

effects.log: You leave it. He dies in his time, and the temple is cleaner after.

events.text: On your festival day, at a thousand temples sharing one lamp, a family of strangers leaves no offering at all. They simply sit on the steps and eat, and talk, and let a child nap with her head on a worn stone. Your qi rises more from that than from the heaped altar.

choices.text: Hush the thousand temples so the nap goes undisturbed

effects.log: A thousand lamps lower together. It is the quietest night of the age.

choices.text: Ask the wardens to keep a respectful distance

effects.log: They do. The family leaves unnoticed and rested.

choices.text: Study the peace the stair gives the dead and the living alike

effects.log: It is the same peace. You write that down.

events.text: Your domain stretches now across a continent's seasons, and a small thing in it happens only because you let it: a late frost holds off, a river changes its mind. You are discovering that a god's power is mostly a list of things they decline to do.

choices.text: Decline one more ending, and note it in the Pale Gallery

effects.log: The ledger gains a line of reprieve. A hundred beds are quieter than they might have been.

choices.text: Reach for one small mercy: a gentler hour for the dying

effects.log: The hour softens, and the room does too. Your power bends like cloth.

choices.text: Walk your continent's seasons and ask what they are owed

effects.log: Autumn asks for patience, winter for company. You promise both.

events.text: Two of your domain's laws have begun to disagree. The same rain that feeds a field drowns a village below it, and you are the only one who can say which matters more. Baekun has offered to hold one of the laws for you while you think.

choices.text: Accept Baekun's offer to hold the law of endings, and think a hundred years

effects.log: They hold it patiently. You think. The answer is neither law.

choices.text: Decide at once, and bear what follows

effects.log: You choose and own it. You attend each funeral that follows, for as long as it takes.

choices.text: Give the question to the village elders and the dead to answer together

effects.log: The living and the dead hold a long hearing. The answer is simple and just.

events.text: A god of the will of heaven asks to see how you keep your domain. They stay a month, taking notes, asking questions, never praising. On the last day they say your domain is the least beautiful they have seen, and the most alive.

choices.text: Thank them; it is high praise in the Will's language

effects.log: They bow, and you bow back. Your visitor goes away surprised to be thanked.

choices.text: Ask what they would change in your Pale Gallery

effects.log: They name three things. You change two, and keep the one that hurts.

choices.text: Return the visit and be unpraised in their Hall

effects.log: You spend a month in the Silent Hall. Nobody says a word. It is wonderful.

events.text: A Revelation arrives over a scriptorium the way weather arrives: not as words, but a rearrangement of the air. You spend a month deciphering it and are left with one phrase you cannot stop turning over, like a stone in the mouth. It seems to be about patience.

choices.text: Study the phrase in the Pale Gallery's quiet until it opens

effects.log: On the twentieth day the quiet answers. You carry the answer out under your arm.

choices.text: Hand it to the copyist, who will never understand it and will copy it perfectly

effects.log: She does. The perfect copy is a Revelation of its own.

choices.text: Keep it and read it only on the day of a funeral

effects.log: It rests until then. When you read it, it fits.

events.text: A manual of the gods has come into your keeping, copied seven times over by seven tired hands. In the margin of the fourth chapter, someone has written in a different ink: "This does not work near a thunderhead." You are not sure if that is a warning or a joke.

choices.text: Try the chapter in a thunderstorm and see if the margin lied

effects.log: It fails loudly, and you see why. You nod at the margin.

choices.text: Ask the copyist who last held the book

effects.log: She has a name, a date, and a rumour. You follow the rumour.

choices.text: Write your own note beside it: "Not even then"

effects.log: Baekun reads it later and says it is the funniest thing in the Gallery.

events.text: In the night a Revelation comes that is not for you. It is meant for a young god of Death, and has simply fallen on the wrong roof, here beside a scriptorium. It is lovely, and it will do you a little good, and it is not yours.

choices.text: Walk it through the Pale Gallery to the young god of Death it was meant for

effects.log: They take it with both hands and weep a little. You tell no one.

choices.text: Have the copyist make a clean copy for you and give them the original

effects.log: You keep the copy and its good. The young god never knows.

choices.text: Keep it

effects.log: It does you good. You hear Baekun not mentioning it.

events.text: A clerk of the Heavenly Court asks you to confirm a line in the Book of Fates: a copyist is to die in their sleep, tonight, at forty. It is a small, ordinary line. You are not required to object. The ink is not quite dry.

choices.text: Confirm it; you are the one who will receive her

effects.log: You confirm, and wait at the Pale Gallery's door with a cup. She arrives surprised and unafraid.

choices.text: Ask for a day, and use it to read the copyist's own page

effects.log: You read how she has copied for forty years. The line is fair, and you let it stand.

choices.text: Decline and tell the clerk why: she has not yet finished a poem

effects.log: The clerk writes it in the margin. She finishes the poem before the hour.

events.text: You are called as a witness before a Judge of Souls. A copyist you once answered with a small mercy stands accused of selling short measure at a scriptorium. Your testimony will not decide, but it will weigh. The Judge asks nothing but "What did you see?" and waits.

choices.text: Tell exactly what you saw in the scriptorium

effects.log: You describe the ledger and the inked short measure. The Judge nods.

choices.text: Ask to see the ledger before you speak

effects.log: It changes one line of your account. The Judge thanks you.

choices.text: Say nothing that is not recorded

effects.log: You read the record aloud and stop. The Judge finds it enough.

events.text: The Court's archivist gives you a rare gift: an hour alone with the Book of Fates, open at your own page. It is blank except for a single line in a small neat hand: "Left open on purpose." You find that this is the most comforting sentence you have read.

choices.text: Close the Book; fate left open is a door to the dead

effects.log: You close it softly. The line stays where it is, like a waiting room.

choices.text: Write a line, and copy it out in the scriptorium before you rub it out

effects.log: You copy it. You rub it out. The copy remains and is yours alone.

choices.text: Ask the archivist whether Baekun has read their own page

effects.log: The archivist says: twice. The rest is silence.

events.text: You spend a century with a thunderhead, the nearest thing to what your Dao answers: you let it slip through your fingers, you taste it, you let it carry you. You discover that the Dao is not the element, but the way the element refuses to be held.

choices.text: Stand under a thunderhead and let it keep its distance

effects.log: It builds, grows loud, and pulls back. You learn thunder by its absence.

choices.text: Cup a little of the storm in your sleeve and carry it home

effects.log: It crackles up your arm and settles down. You keep the crackle in a jar.

choices.text: Ask the thunderhead how it sees an old death

effects.log: It answers in a quiet rumble: slowly.

events.text: You have watched a thunderhead a million times, and today it looks different. It is nothing. It is the same element at a new angle. Your Dao takes a half-step and you are very careful not to move.

choices.text: Hold still while the thunderhead turns

effects.log: A new side of the cloud opens. The step finishes with a distant roll.

choices.text: Follow the new angle up to the cloud's edge

effects.log: You reach a place where the rain begins. You bring back a drop.

choices.text: Write it down in the scriptorium and see what the copyists make of it

effects.log: They copy it faithfully and misread one word, which improves it.

events.text: A child at a scriptorium is playing with a thunderhead, not knowing it. They are doing it badly and joyfully, and a thing you spent a thousand years learning falls out of their hands by accident. You are not sure whether to be annoyed.

choices.text: Watch the child climb a thunderhead of wet sheets on a line

effects.log: She does it badly and with joy. You steal the joy.

choices.text: Send a faint breeze to lift her kite

effects.log: It rises, and she shouts. She never knows why.

choices.text: Leave the child to the weather; it is her lesson

effects.log: You step back. The storm passes, and she is soaked and delighted.

events.text: You are asked to give the opening address at a council of pantheons in the Pale Gallery: a short talk on what a god owes the faithful. The Will of Heaven says order, the Silent Hall says remembrance, the Green Assembly says growth, the Throne of Storms says weight. You must pick, or find a fifth.

choices.text: Say a god owes a good end, and read the names in the Pale Gallery

effects.log: A hush falls. The Silent Hall, for once, applauds.

choices.text: Say a god owes the faithful their records kept true

effects.log: The Will of Heaven nods; the copyist weeps in the gallery.

choices.text: Propose a fifth: a god owes an honest account of the dead

effects.log: The council debates it for a season. A new office is founded.

events.text: A doctrine you have followed for ages turns out, on a close reading, to be a mistranslation: one word (weigh) was swapped by a scribe, and an entire school of devotion built on the swap. The error is beautiful. Correcting it would cost a lot of people their favourite prayer.

choices.text: Publish the correction in the scriptorium at the next copy

effects.log: Every new copy bears the right word. The old copies fade slowly.

choices.text: Footnote it, and let the dead decide which they prefer

effects.log: The dead are polite. A few of them correct you.

choices.text: Keep it quiet; the mourners need that word

effects.log: You say nothing. The mistake comforts the grieving, and your conscience leans on it.

events.text: In the Pale Gallery, a god of the Will of Heaven asks you to explain your doctrine without using any of its words. You try and fail. You try again and succeed halfway. By the end you have learned what you actually believe, which is smaller and truer than the doctrine.

choices.text: Thank them and rewrite your teaching in the copyist's plain hand

effects.log: It reads like a letter. Half your students leave; the rest write back.

choices.text: Admit that the doctrine is a stair and death is the roof

effects.log: They smile, and a candle in the gallery lights itself.

choices.text: Defend the doctrine out of habit

effects.log: You defend it in the Pale Gallery's hush. The visitor leaves unmoved, and you feel the hush.

events.text: You catch yourself at the old etiquette again: calling every god by their old rank. It is a habit from your Upper Realm centuries, and the gods in the Pale Gallery are politely baffled. A cup is just a cup here.

choices.text: Call a god by their new rank and see what happens

effects.log: Nothing happens. A scribe nearby notes that you have been cured.

choices.text: Keep calling them by their old rank; the Gallery likes the history

effects.log: The gallery adopts it. Old ranks become a small art.

choices.text: Study why you cannot let go of the old names

effects.log: You discover a name you meant to say goodbye to. It takes a week.

events.text: You still keep a ledger of favours owed, a leftover of the immortals' exchange. The oldest line is a copied scroll. A god would never keep one, and when a friend sees it they look briefly hurt. The ledger is accurate to the grain, and entirely beside the point.

choices.text: Strike out each line and re-copy only the thanks

effects.log: The new ledger is three pages. You are lighter and poorer.

choices.text: Keep the ledger sealed and leave it to the Gallery after you

effects.log: It sits there. In ten thousand years someone will read it.

choices.text: Add what you owe the dead, line by line

effects.log: The sum is humbling, and long.

events.text: You flinched at a stair today. The Upper Realm taught you to expect a hand behind such things, and the habit lives in the shoulders long after the cause is gone. Here nothing is behind them, and your body has not yet been told.

choices.text: Walk a stair of the Pale Gallery slowly with your back to the drop

effects.log: Nothing is behind you. Your shoulders drop.

choices.text: Ask Baekun what the dead flinch at

effects.log: They say: nothing. It is not comforting, and it helps.

choices.text: Count the steps aloud and stop at the last

effects.log: The last is just a step. You laugh.

events.text: A copyist prays, in a scriptorium, with an ink-stone in their other hand. They do not ask for anything. They only say "thank you for the weather." You, who keep weather, find that nobody has ever thanked you for it before.
